chapters.title: Depression in the Pulpit: A Pastor's Mental Health
chapters.summary: The man who tells your congregation that there is hope can sit in his study on Saturday night unable to find any for himself, and the church has built a theology that makes him hide it.
chapters.body:
I have preached a sermon on the goodness of God on a morning when I could not feel it. I want to begin there, because I am tired of articles about pastoral depression written as though the writer observed it from a clean distance. I did not observe it. I stood in a pulpit with my chest full of lead and told three hundred people about a joy I was, in that hour, unable to locate in myself. Some of you reading this know exactly the weight I mean. You have done it too. We do not talk about it, and the not talking is part of the sickness.

There is a sentence pastors learn to say without believing it. I am fine. We say it in the narthex with a smile that took years to perfect. We say it to elders who would panic if we said anything else. We say it to our wives until our wives stop believing us and start grieving in silence beside us. The smile is a skill, and like every skill it can be practiced until it runs without the soul behind it. A man can be the most fluent liar in his own life, and the lie he tells best is the one about his own condition.

The strongest objection to taking this seriously is theological, and it comes from sincere men, so I will give it its full weight. They say depression in a believer, and especially in a shepherd, is finally a failure of faith. The joy of the Lord is your strength. Rejoice in the Lord always. If a man truly believed the gospel he preaches, the argument goes, he would not be crushed, and to treat his despair as a medical condition is to excuse a spiritual one. I understand the instinct. There is a kind of modern therapy culture that dissolves all sin into syndrome, that lets a man off every hook by renaming every failure a wound. That culture is real and it is wrong, and I will not defend it.

But the argument fails on its own ground, because it cannot survive contact with the Bible it claims to honor. The Psalms are full of men of profound faith in profound despair. Why are you cast down, O my soul, the psalmist asks himself, and the very next breath he is still cast down (Psalm 42:5 ESV). Jeremiah curses the day he was born. Job, whom God Himself calls blameless, longs for death across thirty chapters. And there, again, is Elijah under the broom tree, a man who had just called down fire from heaven, asking God to take his life (1 Kings 19:4 ESV). If despair were always faithlessness, then the most faithful men in Scripture were the most faithless, and that is an absurdity the argument cannot escape. The God of the Bible does not treat Elijah's collapse as sin to be rebuked. He treats it as a body and a soul to be fed.

Let me carry Elijah through, because his story is the truest map I know for this. Read what God does. He does not preach to Elijah. He sends an angel who bakes bread and touches him and says, twice, arise and eat (1 Kings 19:5-7). The first prescription for the despairing prophet is food and sleep. Let that land on the men who think the cure for a depressed pastor is more Scripture memory and a sterner devotional life. Sometimes the holiest thing a crushed man can do is eat a meal and sleep through the night. The body is not a distraction from the soul. The body is where the soul lives, and a body that has not slept in three weeks will lie to a man about God, about hope, about whether the morning is worth rising for.

Then, after the bread and the sleep, God brings Elijah to the mountain and is not in the wind, not in the earthquake, not in the fire, but in a sound of thin silence (1 Kings 19:11-12). I find that almost unbearable in its tenderness. The God who answered Baal's prophets with fire answers His broken servant with quiet. He does not shout at a man who is already on the floor. We could learn to pastor each other that way. We could learn to pastor ourselves that way.

I said I would be inside this and not above it, so here is the inside. There was a winter in my ministry when I sat in my study every Saturday night and could not finish the sermon, not because the text was hard but because I could not assemble a reason to care. I am a man who came to faith out of atheism, and the cruelty of that season was the return of the old silence, the suspicion that the universe was empty after all, arriving now in the very office where I prepared to preach it full. I was raised without a father, and I had spent my life proving I could carry things alone, and depression is the bill that comes due for a man who has never let anyone carry him. I told no one for far too long. I am a pastor. I am supposed to be the one who carries. The pride of that is its own confession.

The history of how the church got here is worth naming, because shame this specific is usually manufactured. For much of the modern era the church inherited a folk theology that read all suffering as either punishment or insufficient faith, and the holiness movements and parts of the revival tradition sharpened it. Then the twentieth century added the cult of the victorious Christian life, the smiling-pastor-as-brand, the platform that punishes any visible weakness with declining attention. Charles Spurgeon, who knew this country well, preached through depression so heavy he sometimes could not leave his bed, and he told his students plainly that fits of depression come over the most of us, that the strong are not always vigorous, the wise not always ready, the brave not always courageous, and the joyous not always happy (Spurgeon 1875). The man Victorian England called the prince of preachers was describing his own broom tree. We forgot him, and built a culture that would have shamed him into silence.

The research confirms what the silence hides. Lifeway Research found that nearly a quarter of pastors have personally struggled with some kind of mental illness, and about half of those said the illness had been diagnosed (Lifeway 2014). A quarter. Look out across the men at your next denominational gathering and do the arithmetic, then remember that the number is almost certainly low, because the instrument was a survey, and pastors have a trained reflex for telling surveys that we are fine.

Here is the reversal that the smiling theology cannot hold. The pastor's despair is not always his disqualification. It is sometimes the very ground of his usefulness, because a man who has been to the floor and found God still there preaches resurrection with a weight that the untouched cannot fake. Henri Nouwen called this the wounded healer, the minister whose own wounds become a source of healing for others, not when they are hidden but when they are made available (Nouwen 1972). The point is not to perform the wound. The point is that a man who has suffered and been met by God in it can sit with a suffering parishioner and not flinch, because he has been in that room and knows the way the light eventually comes in.

Now the cross, and the law before the grace. The law first. If you are hiding your despair to protect your reputation, your reputation has become your idol, and you are willing to drown privately rather than let the body of Christ see that you bleed. That is not humility. That is pride wearing humility's coat, and I have worn it. The grace second. The cross is the place where God Himself entered the dark and cried out that He was forsaken, and that cry means there is no basement of human despair where Christ has not already been. My God, my God, why have you forsaken me (Matthew 27:46 ESV). The man in the pulpit who feels forsaken is not outside the gospel. He is standing exactly where the gospel happened. The Savior went into the silence so that the silence would never again be the final word over a single one of His shepherds.

So tell someone. Not the congregation from the platform, necessarily, but someone. A brother, a physician, a counselor, a friend who will bake the bread and not preach the sermon. The God who fed Elijah is not ashamed of your weakness. The only one ashamed of it is you, and that shame is a liar.

The pulpit is not a place you have to be well to enter. It is a place a wounded man tells the truth about a God who meets the wounded. Be that man. Then go eat something and sleep.

### Works Cited

Lifeway Research. 2014. Study of Acute Mental Illness and Christian Faith. Nashville: Lifeway Research.

Nouwen, Henri J. M. 1972. The Wounded Healer: Ministry in Contemporary Society. New York: Doubleday.

Spurgeon, Charles H. 1875. Lectures to My Students. London: Passmore and Alabaster.

The Holy Bible, English Standard Version. 2001. Wheaton, IL: Crossway.

chapters.title: Expository vs. Topical Preaching: Which and When
chapters.summary: The argument between expository and topical preaching is usually a disguise for a deeper question, which is whether the preacher will submit to a text or use one.
chapters.body:
Two preachers prepare for the same Sunday. The first opens his Bible to where he left off last week, the next paragraph of Romans, and his sermon is decided for him before he has had a single idea, because the text decided it. The second begins with a question that has been pressing on his people, anxiety, money, a marriage falling apart, and he goes looking for the passages that speak to it. By Saturday night both will have a sermon. The question the conferences keep arguing about is which of them did it right. The question underneath, the one that actually matters, is which of them let the Word be in charge.

That is the real fault line, and it does not run cleanly between the two methods. There are expositors who march verse by verse through a book and never once let the text correct them, because they have already decided what each verse will say. And there are topical preachers who chase a theme and end up more captive to Scripture than the expositor, because the theme drove them back into six passages they could not control. Method is not the same as submission. We have spent a generation treating it as though it were.

Let me give the case for expository preaching its full strength, because it is strong and I believe most of it. When a preacher commits to working through a book of the Bible, paragraph by paragraph, he surrenders his right to avoid. He cannot skip the verse about money this autumn because the building campaign is on. He cannot dodge the hard saying about divorce because three couples in the room are in the middle of one. The discipline of the next verse drags him into territory he would never have chosen, and that is precisely its gift. Haddon Robinson built his whole case on this, that the expositor lets the biblical idea, not the preacher's idea, govern the sermon, so that the authority in the room is the text and not the man (Robinson 1980). John Stott went further and said that all true Christian preaching is expository in spirit, because all of it exists to open up the meaning of a text and let it speak (Stott 1982). I will not argue against that. The discipline of the consecutive text has saved more sermons from the preacher's vanity than any other practice I know.

But the strongest form of the expository case has a blind spot, and naming it is not an attack on the method. It is this. The Bible itself does not always preach expositorily. When Peter stands up on the day of Pentecost, he does not open a scroll and work through it verse by verse. He has a topic, and the topic is the thing that just happened in the street, and he reaches for Joel and for two Psalms and for the promise to David, pulling texts from across the canon to answer one question the crowd is screaming (Acts 2:14-36 ESV). That is a topical sermon. It is in the Bible. It converted three thousand people. Whatever rule we are about to make against topical preaching, the apostle broke it on the first day of the church, and the Spirit blessed the breaking.

Carry that Pentecost sermon as the spine, because it teaches the actual rule. Peter's sermon is topical in arrangement and ruthlessly expository in submission. He does not bend the texts to his theme. He lets the texts dictate what the theme is allowed to mean. He quotes Joel and then insists that the strange thing in the street is the very pouring out of the Spirit that Joel saw in the last days (Acts 2:17 ESV). He quotes the Psalm and then refuses to let David claim it for himself, because David died and was buried and his tomb is with us to this day, so the incorruption the Psalm promised must belong to another (Acts 2:29-31 ESV). The topic gave Peter his starting point. The text gave Peter his authority. He did not choose between the two. He ordered them rightly.

This is the distinction the whole argument keeps missing. The danger of topical preaching is real, but it is not the topic. The danger is the proof-text, the verse yanked out of its paragraph to nod along with a point the preacher already owned. The danger of expository preaching is also real, and it is not the consecutive text. The danger is the running commentary, the verse-by-verse march that explains everything and lands nowhere, that mistakes coverage for proclamation. I have committed both sins. I have used a Psalm to prove a thing the Psalm was not saying. I have also walked a congregation through fourteen verses of Leviticus and left them more informed and less pierced than when they came in, and called it faithfulness because it was thorough.

Watch how Peter's submission shows itself, because it is the part we cannot fake. When the crowd, cut to the heart, cries out asking what they should do, Peter does not soften the topic to keep them. He has just told them they crucified the Lord of glory, and now that the wound is open he pours grace into it, repent and be baptized, every one of you (Acts 2:38 ESV). The law came first and it came hard, the plain charge that this Jesus, whom you crucified, God has made both Lord and Christ (Acts 2:36 ESV). The topic did not let Peter dodge that sentence. The topic was the resurrection of a man the crowd had killed, and you cannot preach that topic faithfully without the indictment that makes the grace necessary. So the test of a topical sermon is not whether it began with a theme. The test is whether the theme was allowed to wound before it healed, or whether the preacher reached for a comfortable topic precisely so he would never have to.

The history clarifies why we are so anxious about this. The verse-by-verse expository sermon, the kind associated with the consecutive exposition of a whole book, has deep roots, but its modern American dominance owes much to the twentieth-century reaction against the topical sermon's collapse. By the mid-century the liberal pulpit had so often used a verse as a springboard into the preacher's own opinions that conservatives recoiled toward the text and would not let go. The recoil was justified. The springboard sermon deserved to die. But a recoil is not a doctrine. We turned a healthy correction into an absolute, and we began to speak as though Spurgeon, who almost never preached consecutively through a book and took a single text wherever it served the wounded soul in front of him, had somehow been doing it wrong (Spurgeon 1875). Spurgeon was not doing it wrong.

So when each. Preach the consecutive book when your people need to be confronted with the whole counsel of God and cannot be allowed to live on the preacher's favorite forty verses. Preach the consecutive book when you yourself are the danger, when your instinct to avoid the hard text needs a stronger master than your instinct. That is most seasons. But preach topically when a death has torn through the congregation and the next paragraph of your series has nothing to say to it, because to ignore the open grave in the room in order to protect your schedule is to love the method more than the people. Preach topically when the culture has put a question to the church that the church is fumbling, and the answer is scattered across the canon and has to be gathered. Phillips Brooks said the truth must come through a personality that has been changed by it (Brooks 1877). A method cannot be changed by anything. Only a man can.

There is also an honesty the method debate lets us avoid, and it is about why we choose what we choose. I have hidden inside the expository series for reasons that had nothing to do with the whole counsel of God. A long series is a long permission to coast. The decisions are made for the year, the trajectory is set, and a tired man can lean on the structure the way a tired man leans on a wall. I have likewise reached for a topical sermon not because a grave had opened but because the next paragraph of Romans frightened me and a softer subject was available. The method was a costume in both cases. Underneath the costume was the same man making the same choice, which was the choice to spare himself. No method will save you from that choice. The consecutive text can become an alibi as easily as the topic can become an escape. The question is never which method is faithful. The question is which one, this Saturday, you are using to hide.

And in both, the cross has to do its work, and the law has to come before the grace. The expositor can hide from this behind his careful verbs and his Greek, ending the sermon in the lexicon instead of at the foot of the cross. The topical preacher can hide from it behind relevance, scratching the felt need so gently that no one is ever cut. Both evasions leave the room comfortable. Neither method protects you from the one failure that matters, which is preaching about a text instead of letting the text preach to you first and then through you to them.

Do not ask which method is holy. Ask which one, this week, makes you submit.

### Works Cited

Brooks, Phillips. 1877. Lectures on Preaching. New York: E. P. Dutton.

Robinson, Haddon W. 1980. Biblical Preaching. Grand Rapids: Baker.

Spurgeon, Charles H. 1875. Lectures to My Students. London: Passmore and Alabaster.

Stott, John R. W. 1982. Between Two Worlds. Grand Rapids: Eerdmans.

chapters.title: Five Preaching Habits That Empty a Room
chapters.summary: A room does not usually empty all at once, it leaks, one Sunday at a time, through habits the preacher cannot see because he is the one performing them.
chapters.body:
No one walks out in the middle of a sermon. That is not how a room empties. It empties slowly, over months, through a thousand small decisions made in cars on the way home, the decision that next week can wait, that the children have a game, that nothing will be lost by missing it. The preacher rarely sees the leak because the leak is silent and because he is standing at the exact spot where it begins. I have emptied rooms. Not with scandal. With habits I could not see in myself because I was the one doing them.

Before the list, the strongest objection, and it is one I half believe. A faithful preacher should not be managing the room at all. The numbers are the Spirit's business. Noah preached for decades and saved eight. Jeremiah cleared the building every week and was right every week. If you start preaching to keep people, you will stop preaching the truth, because the truth empties rooms on purpose, and the cross was the emptiest room in history, down to a few women and a borrowed tomb. There is real steel here. The preacher who counts heads will eventually trim the gospel to fit the heads he wants to keep, and a trimmed gospel is no gospel. I hold that with both hands.

But the objection proves less than it claims, because there is a difference between a room emptied by the offense of the cross and a room emptied by the offense of the preacher. Jesus said the word would divide households and that men would hate his disciples for his name (Matthew 10:22 ESV). He did not promise they would hate us for being boring. When people leave because the gospel cut them, that is the cost of faithfulness. When they leave because the man in front of them mistook his habits for the gospel, that is not a cross. That is a waste, and we have learned to baptize our waste by calling it persecution. So examine the habits, and be honest about which kind of emptying you are causing.

The self-deception here is comfortable, which is why it lasts. A man whose preaching is dull can read the parable of the sower and decide his hearers are simply the path, the rocky soil, the thorns, and that the seed was fine all along. The parable gives him cover, because it is true that some hearts are hard. But the same parable says the sower scatters, and a sower who has fallen asleep against the fence post is not faithfully losing seed to bad soil. He is just asleep. I have used the doctrine of the hardened heart to explain away rooms that I myself bored into the parking lot. The doctrine is real. My use of it was a lie. Discernment begins with refusing to let a true doctrine cover a false comfort, and the five habits below are five comforts I have hidden behind.

The first habit is preaching to no one. The sermon is built for a congregation that does not exist, the general Christian, the person in general, and so it lands on no actual chest in the room. Haddon Robinson warned that a sermon must aim its single idea at the real lives present, not at humanity in the abstract (Robinson 1980). The abstract sermon is safe, because no one feels named, and that safety is the leak. The woman whose son will not speak to her did not come to hear about reconciliation in general. She came in case God had a word for that, the specific grave she is carrying, and the general sermon tells her, week after gentle week, that he does not.

The second habit is explaining when you should be proclaiming. The preacher becomes a lecturer, accumulating information about the text, the Greek, the historical setting, the cross-references, until the sermon is a seminar with a prayer at each end. The people leave knowing more and feeling nothing, and a person who feels nothing will eventually decide that nothing is at stake. Fred Craddock noticed that the church had trained preachers to explain the gospel so thoroughly that they forgot to announce it (Craddock 1971). Information is not proclamation. You can teach a man the chemistry of bread and leave him starving.

The third habit is the sermon with no spine. It has parts, and the parts are each true, but they are stapled together rather than grown from one root, and the listener cannot carry any of it out because there was no single thing to carry. The mind does not retain a list. It retains a thrust. When a sermon has three good points and no governing idea, the people remember that the preacher was earnest and forget what he was earnest about, and a thing forgotten by Tuesday is a thing that will not bring them back by Sunday.

The fourth habit is the soft landing, and this one I committed most. The sermon builds, the law presses, the text has the listener cornered, and then at the last moment the preacher loses his nerve and lets everyone off easy. A comfortable closing. A reassurance that softens the very thing the text spent its force to say. Walter Brueggemann argued that the prophetic sermon must not resolve the tension it raises but leave the hearer standing in it, because a too-quick comfort robs the word of its power to change anything (Brueggemann 1989). The soft landing is the preacher protecting the room from the text and the text from the room, and the room can feel the protection, and the protection is condescension wearing the mask of grace. People do not return to a place that keeps telling them nothing is wrong.

The fifth habit is the borrowed self. The preacher steps into the pulpit and becomes someone else, a pulpit voice, a pulpit cadence, a borrowed certainty that belongs to no one in his actual life. Phillips Brooks defined the whole enterprise as truth through personality, and he meant that the truth has to pass through a real person who has been changed by it, not through a performance of a person (Brooks 1877). When the self in the pulpit is borrowed, the people sense the gap without naming it. They feel handled. They cannot say why they distrust the man, only that they do, and distrust is a slow exit. The cross was the most personal thing God ever did, a body, named, on a Friday, and we announce it through a mask.

There is a sixth thing under the five, and it is worth naming because it explains why the habits cluster. A man does not usually pick up these habits one at a time, like bad swings in golf. He picks them up together, all at once, the first time the pulpit frightens him. The fear is reasonable. To preach is to stand up and claim that God is speaking, and that claim invites a judgment no other public speech invites. So the frightened man reaches, almost without deciding, for every available shelter. He generalizes so no one is named. He explains so he can hide behind data. He multiplies points so no single one can be wrong. He softens the ending so the room will not turn on him. He puts on a voice so that if they reject the sermon they are only rejecting the voice and not the man. Five habits, one fear, and the fear is the fear of being seen failing at the most exposed task a person can attempt.

Notice what all five share. Each is a way of avoiding contact. The abstract sermon avoids the particular person. The lecture avoids the demand to proclaim. The spineless sermon avoids the one hard thing. The soft landing avoids the wound. The borrowed self avoids the cost of being known. Every emptying habit is the preacher protecting himself, and the room leaves because it can smell the self-protection, even from the back row, even through the music.

So carry one text out of this. Paul tells the Thessalonians that he was ready to share not only the gospel but his own self, because they had become dear to him (1 Thessalonians 2:8 ESV). That is the cure for all five at once. The shared self is particular, so it cannot preach to no one. It proclaims, because it is not hiding behind data. It has a spine, because a person under conviction speaks of one thing. It does not soften the landing, because a man who loves you will tell you the truth that costs. And it is not borrowed, because it is his own self he is handing over. The room does not empty around a preacher who is willing to be known.

The habits that empty a room are all the same habit. Hiding.

### Works Cited

Brooks, Phillips. 1877. Lectures on Preaching. New York: E. P. Dutton.

Brueggemann, Walter. 1989. Finally Comes the Poet. Minneapolis: Fortress Press.

Craddock, Fred B. 1971. As One Without Authority. Nashville: Abingdon Press.

Robinson, Haddon W. 1980. Biblical Preaching. Grand Rapids: Baker.

chapters.title: How to Build a Healthy Church Staff Culture
chapters.summary: The staff culture you actually have is the one you tolerate on a Tuesday, not the one you describe in the elder retreat.
chapters.body:
A staff meeting opens with prayer, and three of the five people praying are afraid of the person leading it. They are not afraid he will yell. They are afraid of something quieter than that. They are afraid of the look that crosses his face when someone disagrees, the way the temperature in the room drops two degrees, the email that comes at nine that night with the subject line that just says 'Quick thought.' So they pray, and they smile, and they keep the real conversation for the parking lot. The culture of that staff is not the printed values on the breakroom wall. The culture is what happens in the parking lot.

Most pastors think they are building a healthy staff culture when what they are building is a comfortable one. The two are not the same. A comfortable culture is a place where nobody contradicts the leader and everyone leaves on time and the conflict goes underground where it ferments. A healthy culture is a place where the hardest thing on the table gets said by the person least afraid to say it, and nobody loses standing for saying it. I have run both kinds. I know the difference from the inside, because for years I mistook the silence in my own staff meetings for peace, and it was not peace. It was the absence of trust dressed up as agreement.

Let me steel-man the comfortable manager, because he is not a villain and he is often me. He has read the studies. He knows that turnover in ministry is brutal, that pastors burn out, that a church split can take a decade to heal. So he protects the calm. He smooths the friction. He tells himself that a peaceful staff is a faithful staff, that unity is a fruit of the Spirit, that he is shepherding tender people through a hard calling. And he is right about the tenderness. He is right that people in ministry carry wounds that the corporate world does not see. The instinct to protect them is a good instinct that has been pointed in the wrong direction.

Here is what he gets wrong. He has confused the absence of conflict with the presence of trust, and Patrick Lencioni spent a career showing that these are nearly opposites (Lencioni 2002). Trust is what makes conflict survivable. Where trust is high, people fight about ideas in the open and walk out of the room intact. Where trust is low, people agree in the room and undermine in the hallway. The peaceful staff the comfortable manager is so proud of is not a sign of trust. It is a sign that trust is so thin nobody dares to test it. He is not protecting his people. He is starving them of the one thing that would let them tell him the truth.

The spine text here is the night before the cross, and it is stranger than we let it be. 'Jesus, knowing that the Father had given all things into his hands, and that he had come from God and was going to God, rose from supper. He laid aside his outer garments, and taking a towel, tied it around his waist' (John 13:3-4 ESV). Read the logic of that sentence. John tells us first that Jesus knew the full extent of his authority, that everything had been placed in his hands, and then, because of that knowledge and not in spite of it, he got on the floor and washed twelve sets of dirty feet. The security came first. The service came out of the security. He could kneel because there was nothing left to prove.

That is the engine of a healthy staff culture, and almost nobody runs on it. The leader who knows where his standing comes from can take the lowest seat in the room without losing himself. The leader who does not know is the one who needs the meeting to affirm him, who cannot let a critique pass without correcting the record, who washes nobody's feet because he is still waiting for someone to wash his. A church staff inherits the anxiety of the person at the top. If the senior leader is grasping, the whole staff grasps. If he can kneel, he gives them permission to stop performing.

We did not get here by accident, and the history matters. The modern church staff is a young invention. For most of Christian history the local congregation had a pastor and perhaps a sexton, and the idea of an executive pastor, a creative director, a connections coordinator, and a discipleship pastor reporting through an org chart would have been unintelligible. The multi-staff church as we know it is largely a product of the church growth movement that took shape in the nineteen seventies and eighties, when Donald McGavran's work at Fuller and the rise of the seeker-sensitive megachurch taught a generation to think of the congregation as an organization to be scaled. We imported the org chart from the corporation, and with it we imported the corporation's diseases, the politics, the performance reviews, the quiet anxiety of people whose livelihood depends on a manager's mood.

None of that is wrong in itself. Structure is a gift. But we adopted the structure without adopting the safeguard, and the safeguard is theological, not managerial. Edwin Friedman, a rabbi who spent his life studying leadership in congregations and families, named the missing piece. He called it self-differentiation, the capacity of a leader to stay connected to people while staying clear about his own convictions, to hold steady in the presence of someone else's anxiety without absorbing it or reacting to it (Friedman 2007). The differentiated leader does not need the staff to be calm in order to be calm himself. That is what lets him invite the hard conversation. He can hear it without coming apart.

So what do you actually do. Begin with the thing you can control, which is your own face in the room. Watch what happens to the temperature when someone disagrees with you, and learn to keep it level on purpose, because the staff is reading you for permission and you are giving it whether you mean to or not. Then make the disagreement count for something. When a junior staff member tells you a plan will not work and she is right, change the plan in front of everyone and say out loud who changed your mind. Nothing teaches a staff that candor is safe faster than watching candor win once. Bonhoeffer warned that the leader who arrives with a vision of the perfect community and demands that the real people conform to it will end up destroying both the vision and the people (Bonhoeffer 1954). Lead the staff you have, not the one in your head.

And ration your reactions. Henri Nouwen wrote that the great temptation of Christian leadership is the temptation to be relevant, to be spectacular, to be powerful, and that the antidote is a leadership that descends rather than climbs, that is willing to be led where it would rather not go (Nouwen 1989). A healthy staff culture is built by a leader who has made peace with not being the most impressive person in the room. He does not need the win in every exchange. He has already washed feet. He has nothing to prove and therefore everything to give.

There is a test for whether the culture is actually changing, and it is a quiet one. Listen for what your newest and least powerful staff member is willing to say in front of the room. The intern, the part-time administrator, the young hire who joined six months ago and has the most to lose by speaking. When that person disagrees with you out loud, without lowering her voice and without checking the faces of the older staff first, you have built something real. Until that day, every assurance that your people feel free to speak is a thing you are telling yourself, not a thing they have shown you. The health of a staff is measured at its bottom, not its top, the same way Jesus measured greatness on the night he reached for the towel.

The culture you have is the one your people describe in the parking lot. You will not change it with a values document or a ropes course or a verse on the wall. You will change it the first time someone says the dangerous true thing in the meeting and watches you receive it without flinching. That is the whole work, and it never ends. The towel does not stay tied. You pick it up again every Tuesday.

A healthy staff is not a quiet one. It is a brave one.

### Works Cited

Bonhoeffer, Dietrich. 1954. Life Together. Translated by John W. Doberstein. New York: Harper and Row.

Friedman, Edwin H. 2007. A Failure of Nerve: Leadership in the Age of the Quick Fix. New York: Seabury Books.

Lencioni, Patrick. 2002. The Five Dysfunctions of a Team. San Francisco: Jossey-Bass.

Nouwen, Henri J. M. 1989. In the Name of Jesus: Reflections on Christian Leadership. New York: Crossroad.

chapters.title: How to Develop Leaders, Not Just Recruit Volunteers
chapters.summary: A church can run a hundred volunteers through its slots for a decade and produce not a single leader, and most of them do.
chapters.body:
Every September the same announcement goes up on the screen and into the bulletin and across the platform. We need volunteers. The nursery is short, the parking team is thin, the connections desk has two people doing the work of five, and so the ask goes out, and a few tired saints raise their hands again because they always do. The church fills its slots. The machine runs another year. And if you stood at the back of that room and asked who among these faithful people is being formed into a leader who could one day carry weight, the honest answer would be almost none of them, because nobody is trying to.

There is a difference between recruiting and developing, and most churches have collapsed it without noticing. Recruiting fills a need that the church has. Developing meets a need that the person has, the need to grow into the fullness of what God made them to carry. Recruiting asks what the volunteer can do for the ministry. Developing asks what the ministry can do for the volunteer, what God might be building in a human being through the assignment. We say we want to develop leaders. What we usually want is to fill the schedule, and the schedule, once filled, has no reason to develop anyone.

Let me make the recruiter's case honestly, because the work is real and the recruiter is not lazy. The services do have to happen. The children do have to be safe. Someone does have to count the offering and run the slides and stack the chairs, and a church that romanticizes development while the practical work falls apart is not deep, it is just disorganized. The recruiter is keeping the lights on. He looks at the gap between the work and the workers and he closes it the only way he knows how, week after week, and the church owes him more thanks than it gives. His instinct to staff the need is not wrong.

But he has accepted a quiet exchange that is hollowing his church out from the inside. By treating people as labor to be deployed, he gets the slot filled this week and loses the leader who would have filled a hundred slots over twenty years. He is harvesting and never planting. And there is a deeper cost, because people can tell when they are being used rather than formed. The volunteer who senses that the church only wants his hands and not his growth eventually burns out, not from the labor but from the meaninglessness of labor that leads nowhere. We wonder why we cannot keep volunteers. It is because we never made them into anything. We just spent them.

The text I want to carry is the way Jesus made leaders, because it is almost the opposite of how we do it. 'And he appointed twelve, so that they might be with him and he might send them out to preach' (Mark 3:14 ESV). Read the order. With him first. Sent out second. The being with came before the doing for, and the doing flowed out of the being with. Jesus did not recruit twelve volunteers to staff a movement. He drew twelve men into his life, let them watch him pray and weep and argue and rest, and only out of that shared life did he send them to do anything. The formation was relational before it was functional. We have inverted the order, and the inversion is the whole problem.

The history of how we lost this is the history of the church learning to think like a business, and the year markers are not subtle. When the church growth movement took hold across the nineteen seventies and eighties, and Peter Drucker, the most influential management thinker of the century, began consulting with megachurch pastors and teaching them to run congregations as organizations to be scaled, we gained efficiency and lost apprenticeship. The org chart replaced the rabbi. We built systems to process volunteers at scale, intake forms and ministry placement matrices and the language of human capital, and a system that processes people efficiently is structurally incapable of doing the slow, inefficient, deeply personal work of forming one leader at a time. The factory cannot raise a child.

Here is the reversal that costs the most to accept. Developing leaders will always look less efficient than recruiting volunteers, and it will always produce more in the end. Pouring eighteen months into one person who might lead a ministry someday is a worse use of a Tuesday than filling six open slots, by every metric your dashboard tracks. But the six slots are filled by people who will leave, and the one person becomes someone who fills slots you will never see, who develops others, who is still leading when you are gone. The kingdom does not scale the way a corporation scales. It scales the way a vineyard scales, slowly, through roots, one planting at a time, and you will not see the harvest in the quarter you planted it.

What does developing actually require of us, and why do we avoid it. It requires proximity, the willingness to let people close enough to watch you lead and to be coached inside the real work rather than in a classroom. Ruth Haley Barton argues that leaders can only give away what they themselves have received, that an unformed leader produces unformed followers, that the inner life of the one doing the developing is the ceiling on everyone he develops (Barton 2008). This is why we avoid it. Developing a leader means being watched up close, and being watched up close means being known, and being known means our own gaps come into view. Recruiting keeps people at arm's length. Developing brings them inside, where they can see us, and that is precisely the cost we do not want to pay.

It also requires that we hand over real authority before the person is fully ready, which terrifies the recruiter, because real authority handed over means real mistakes made in public. But there is no other way it has ever worked. Jesus sent the twelve out while they still misunderstood almost everything, and they came back having done the work badly and well, and the sending was the school. We hoard the meaningful decisions and then wonder why nobody around us has grown. You cannot develop a leader by letting him stack chairs. You develop him by letting him lead, and then standing close enough to debrief the wreckage and the wins, week after week, until the day he is leading better than you.

The deepest part is the part we are most tempted to skip, the formation of the person beneath the function. Bonhoeffer reminded us that Christian community is not an ideal we impose but a reality we receive, that the goal is never to build the impressive thing but to serve the actual person God has placed in front of us (Bonhoeffer 1954). Developing a leader is finally an act of love for that specific human being, not a strategy for staffing the church. The moment it becomes a strategy, the person feels it, and the formation dies. We must want the volunteer to grow even if it means he grows right out of our church and into a calling we never get the credit for.

The oldest picture of this is not Jesus and the twelve. It is Moses in the wilderness and the day his father-in-law watched him work. Jethro found Moses sitting alone from morning to evening while the people stood around him waiting, judging every dispute himself, and he said the thing every overfunctioning leader needs to hear, what you are doing is not good, you and the people will wear yourselves out, for the thing is too heavy for you and you are not able to do it alone (Exodus 18:17-18 ESV). Then he told Moses to develop leaders, to look for able men out of the people and place them over thousands and hundreds and fifties and tens, to teach them the statutes and let them carry the lighter cases so that they would bear the burden with him (Exodus 18:21-22 ESV). Read what the cure for Moses was. Not a better schedule. Not a more efficient docket. Other leaders, formed and trusted and handed real weight, because the work was never meant to live or die on one man. You will not develop leaders from behind a desk handing out assignments. You develop them the way Jethro told Moses to, by raising up able people, teaching them, and giving them the cases that are too small for your ego and exactly the right size for their growth.

There is a final cost most of us never count, and it is the cost to our own ego. The leader who develops other leaders is signing up to be eclipsed. The people you raise well will, if you have done it faithfully, eventually preach better than you preached at their age, lead larger than you led, see things you cannot see. And a great deal of what passes for a shortage of leaders in our churches is actually a senior leader's quiet unwillingness to be surpassed, a hoarding of the spotlight dressed up as a concern for readiness. We keep people in the volunteer pool because a developed leader is a threat to the man at the top in a way a chair-stacker never will be. Nouwen warned that the descending way of Jesus runs directly against the climbing instinct that lives in every leader, that we are forever tempted to grasp at relevance and visibility instead of giving them away (Nouwen 1989). You cannot develop a leader and protect your own prominence at the same time. You have to choose, and most of us choose ourselves and call it prudence.

This is where the cross has to do its work, and it does it as law before it does it as grace. The law first. The reason you will not raise leaders who might surpass you is that you need to be the indispensable one, the source the church cannot do without, and that need is not humility wearing thin, it is idolatry, the determination to be a small savior to people who already have a real one. You have made your own irreplaceability into a god, and like every idol it demands that everyone around you stay smaller than you so that you can keep feeling large. That is sin, and naming it as sin is the only thing that loosens its grip. The grace second. The cross says the one indispensable work was already finished by the only indispensable Man, accomplished in blood you did not spill while you contributed nothing but the sin he carried, and your standing was settled there before you developed a single leader. You do not have to be the source. You were never the source. The man who has heard that law and received that grace can pour himself into people who will eclipse him and rejoice when they do, because his worth was never riding on being the largest one in the room. He is free to give his power away, because the verdict over him was never his to earn and is no longer his to lose.

A church that only recruits will always be short of volunteers. A church that develops will one day have more leaders than it knows what to do with. Almost all of us are running the first kind and praying for the results of the second.

Stop filling slots. Start raising leaders.

### Works Cited

Barton, Ruth Haley. 2008. Strengthening the Soul of Your Leadership: Seeking God in the Crucible of Ministry. Downers Grove: InterVarsity Press.

Bonhoeffer, Dietrich. 1954. Life Together. Translated by John W. Doberstein. New York: Harper and Row.

Nouwen, Henri J. M. 1989. In the Name of Jesus: Reflections on Christian Leadership. New York: Crossroad.

chapters.title: How to Lead Without Losing Your Soul
chapters.summary: A man can gain a thriving church and lose the very soul that was supposed to lead it, and most of the practices we call leadership are how he does it.
chapters.body:
Jesus asked a question once that every ambitious pastor should have tattooed somewhere he reads it daily. What does it profit a man to gain the whole world and forfeit his soul (Mark 8:36 ESV). He was not speaking to stockbrokers. He was speaking to disciples, to men who wanted to be great, and the warning lands hardest on those of us whose whole world is the work of God. A pastor can forfeit his soul building a kingdom and call the forfeiture sacrifice.

I have watched it happen, and I have felt it happening in myself, which is the only reason I am allowed to write about it. There is a way of leading a church that slowly hollows out the man leading it, and the tragedy is that it often looks like success from the outside. The attendance climbs. The staff grows. The man is busy, sought after, effective. And inside, the well that fed all of it is running dry, and he is preaching from memory of a God he used to know rather than communion with the God he has.

Let me steel-man the resistance, because there is a real and good objection to a whole genre of writing about pastoral self-tending. The objection says that ministry is meant to cost. The shepherd lays down his life for the sheep. Paul poured himself out as a drink offering and counted it joy. There is a modern obsession with the leader's wellness that can become a thin gospel of comfort, a way of dressing up self-protection as wisdom, and a pastor who is forever guarding his peace will never go to the hospital at two in the morning, never absorb the abuse a flock sometimes inflicts on the one who loves them. Sacrifice is not the disease. Sacrifice is the calling. I believe that, and I will not retreat from it.

But the objection mistakes the thing being protected. The argument I am making is not that a pastor should spend himself less. It is that he must be filled from a source that the spending cannot empty, or the spending becomes suicide rather than sacrifice. There is a difference between a candle and a battery. A candle gives light by consuming itself, and when it is gone it is gone. The pastor is not called to be a candle. He is called to be a branch on a vine, abiding, drawing life from a root, giving fruit precisely because he himself is being fed. Cut the branch off and tell it to bear fruit through sheer sacrificial will, and you get a dead stick that produces nothing and calls its barrenness devotion.

So I will carry one text, the vine, through this whole piece. Abide in me, and I in you. As the branch cannot bear fruit by itself, unless it abides in the vine, neither can you, unless you abide in me (John 15:4 ESV). Read the next line, the one we skip. Apart from me you can do nothing (John 15:5). Nothing. Not less. Nothing. Jesus did not say apart from Him we can do a reduced amount of slightly weaker ministry. He said the works of a disconnected branch amount to zero, no matter how impressive the branch looks while it withers. The most frightening possibility in pastoral ministry is a man building something large and fruitless, a great visible nothing, because he severed himself from the vine in order to have more time to produce fruit.

I know the severing intimately. I came to faith out of atheism, and converts often carry a fear that the whole thing depends on their effort, because they remember a time when there was no grace holding them and they survived on will alone. I was raised without a father, so I learned early that love had to be earned and that rest was for men who could afford it. Put those two facts in a pastor and you get a machine. For years I treated abiding as a luxury I would get to once the work was under control, which is to say never, because the work is never under control. I was a branch trying to manufacture sap. I produced a great deal of activity and was, in the years I am least proud of, doing nothing.

The history of how we got here has a shape worth tracing. The modern leadership-pastor is a relatively recent invention. Through the twentieth century, and especially from the 1970s forward, the American church absorbed the language and the instincts of corporate management. The pastor became the visionary, the leader, the CEO of a religious enterprise, and the seminaries followed, adding leadership tracks and strategic planning to curricula that once taught prayer and the cure of souls. Eugene Peterson watched this happen and named it as a betrayal of the office. He said pastors had become a company of shopkeepers, and the shops they kept were churches, busy with the trivia of religious commerce, asking how to keep the customers happy, how to lure customers away from competitors, how to package the goods (Peterson 1987). The work of attending to God in the depths got crowded out by the work of running the store. And a man can run a very good store and lose his soul behind the counter.

I want to press on the word abide, because it is the verb the whole vine passage turns on, and it is the verb we are worst at. To abide is not to visit. A man does not abide in a place he stops by between appointments. He abides where he lives, where he returns at the end of every day, where his deepest sense of home is located. Jesus is describing a continuous dwelling, a settled communion that does not switch off when the sermon is finished and the office locks. And the test of whether a man is abiding is not how he performs on Sunday. The test is what happens in his soul on the ordinary Thursday when nothing is required of him, whether his instinct is to run back to the vine or to run to the next task. I have failed that test for whole seasons of my ministry, abiding in the work and merely visiting the Lord, and the fruit of those seasons looked alive on the branch and was already dying at the stem.

There is a cost to admitting this in front of other pastors, and the cost is the very thing that keeps us silent. We are supposed to be the men who have figured out the life with God, who teach others to abide. To confess that we ourselves have been severed branches running on stored sap feels like disqualification. It is not. Bonhoeffer, writing for a community of pastors under pressure, insisted that the man who cannot be alone with God should beware of community, and the man who cannot bear community should beware of being alone, that the two are bound together and a failure in one corrupts the other (Bonhoeffer 1954). The pastor who has no interior solitude with God brings only his anxious, performing self into the life of the church, and the church feels it, even when it cannot name it.

Here is the reversal, and it cuts against everything the leadership industry sells. The most useful thing a pastor does for his people is often the thing that produces nothing visible at all. The hour of prayer that fills no seats. The day of rest that the calendar resents. Edwin Friedman, a rabbi and family therapist, argued that the single most important variable in a leader's effectiveness is not technique but the leader's own differentiated, non-anxious presence, his capacity to stay connected to people while not being absorbed and driven by their anxiety (Friedman 1999). A pastor who has not tended his own interior life becomes a tuning fork for every fear in the congregation, vibrating with the room, unable to lead because he has no ground to lead from. The interior work is not retreat from leadership. It is the precondition of leadership that does not destroy the leader.

Now the cross, law first. The law exposes the lie under the workaholism, and the lie is this. You do not actually believe the work is God's. If you believed God builds the house, you would be able to sleep while He builds it, and your inability to rest is a sermon you are preaching to yourself every day about who you really think is in charge. Unless the Lord builds the house, those who build it labor in vain (Psalm 127:1 ESV). The verse goes on to say He gives to his beloved sleep. Your insomnia is a doctrine. I have preached that false doctrine to myself for years, and it is a denial of the gospel dressed as diligence.

The grace second. The cross means the decisive work is already finished, accomplished by Another, signed in blood you did not spill. It is finished, He said, and He meant it, and your frantic addition to a completed work is not piety, it is unbelief (John 19:30 ESV). The gospel frees a man to labor hard precisely because his identity does not ride on the labor. He can pour himself out at the hospital bed at two in the morning and then sleep without guilt, because the sleep is not laziness, it is faith that the vine keeps feeding the branch while the branch rests.

The soul is not a resource you spend on the church. It is the place where you meet the God who sends you to the church, and if you spend it, you have nothing left to send.

Guard the root. Let the fruit take care of itself.

### Works Cited

Bonhoeffer, Dietrich. 1954. Life Together. Translated by John W. Doberstein. New York: Harper and Row.

Friedman, Edwin H. 1999. A Failure of Nerve: Leadership in the Age of the Quick Fix. New York: Seabury Books.

Peterson, Eugene H. 1987. Working the Angles: The Shape of Pastoral Integrity. Grand Rapids: Eerdmans.

The Holy Bible, English Standard Version. 2001. Wheaton, IL: Crossway.

chapters.title: How to Preach to People Who Have Heard It All
chapters.summary: The hardest congregation is not the hostile one but the one that has already heard your text a hundred times and stopped expecting anything from it.
chapters.body:
A woman sits in the fourth pew on a Sunday in February, and she has heard this passage before. She has heard it from you. She has heard it from the man who stood there before you. She heard it at the camp she went to in 1994 and at the funeral of her mother and on a podcast last Tuesday while she folded laundry. You announce the text and her face does a small, courteous thing. It closes. Not in anger. In recognition. She knows where this is going, and she is already three steps ahead of you, waiting at the application like a commuter who has memorized the route.

This is the real difficulty of preaching in a country soaked in two centuries of sermons. Not unbelief. Familiarity. The skeptic at least arrives curious about whether the thing is true. The veteran believer arrives certain that he already knows what you are about to say, and his certainty is the wall. I have stood in front of that wall most Sundays of my life. I built part of it myself, every week I told people what they expected to hear in the order they expected to hear it.

The strongest case against worrying about this comes from the deepest part of the tradition, and it deserves a fair hearing. The Reformed instinct says the preacher is not in the entertainment business. The Word does its own work. Faith comes by hearing, and the hearing is of the Word of Christ (Romans 10:17 ESV). If the gospel feels familiar, that is no defect of the gospel. It is the patient repetition by which the Spirit wears a groove into the soul. The manna fell every morning and it was always manna. To chase novelty is to insult the bread. There is real truth here, and I will not pretend otherwise. The preacher who only wants to surprise people has already left the pulpit for the stage. Repetition is not the enemy. Familiarity is not the enemy.

But answer the strongest version of the objection honestly, and it splits. The manna was the same substance, yes. It was never the same morning. The problem in the fourth pew is not that the woman has heard the truth too often. The problem is that she has heard it explained too often and encountered it too rarely. We have handed people summaries of the text instead of the text. We have told them what the passage means so efficiently that they have never once been made to stand inside it and feel the floor give way.

Carry one text. Luke gives us a road. Two men walking away from Jerusalem on the afternoon of the resurrection, talking about the very events that had just shattered them, and the risen Christ falls into step beside them, and they do not know him (Luke 24:13-16 ESV). These are not skeptics. They are insiders. They had hoped he was the one to redeem Israel. They knew the prophecies. They had heard it all. And the Lord himself, walking beside them, does not begin by announcing who he is. He asks them a question. What are you discussing as you walk along. He makes them say the familiar thing out loud until they hear how it sounds in their own grief, and only then, beginning with Moses and all the Prophets, does he open the Scriptures they had known since childhood. Their hearts burned. The text had not changed. The road had been walked before. Something else happened.

What happened was that the familiar material was taken back from them and given again as if for the first time. This is the preacher's task with the over-catechized. Not new information. Re-encounter. Fred Craddock saw this clearly when he argued that the old deductive sermon, which announces its conclusion and then defends it, hands the hearer a verdict before the hearer has lived the case (Craddock 1971). The woman in the fourth pew has the verdict already. She does not need it restated. She needs to be walked back through the evidence until the verdict becomes hers again, earned in the body, not received in the ear.

Consider how the Lord does it on that road, because the method is the message. He withholds. He could have ended the conversation in one sentence at the first mile, named himself, settled the grief, and the two men would have gone home with a fact and a fading wonder. Instead he chooses the long way. He lets them grieve out loud. He lets them recite the very hope they had buried, that they had hoped he was the one to redeem Israel, and he lets the past tense of that sentence hang in the air. He even reproaches them, calling them slow of heart to believe all that the prophets had spoken (Luke 24:25 ESV), which is a harder word than we would dare give the wounded. And only after the reproach, after the recitation, after the slow reopening of texts they had memorized as children, does he break the bread and let their eyes come open. He preached the long sermon when the short answer was available, because the short answer would have been survivable and the long one was not.

Here the history of preaching has a warning for us, and it is specific. By the late nineteenth century, much of American Protestant preaching had become what Phillips Brooks, lecturing at Yale in 1877, feared most. He defined preaching as truth through personality, and he meant that the truth had to pass through a living person who had been altered by it (Brooks 1877). A generation later the alteration was optional. The sermon became a delivery system for points. Three of them, alliterated, with an illustration apiece. The form was so predictable that the congregation could fill in the blanks. We taught people to anticipate us, and then we blamed them for being bored.

The machinery that made the sermon predictable was not laziness. It was efficiency, and efficiency is the enemy here. A revival culture that needed to move crowds quickly learned to compress the gospel into a portable formula, a few verses, a decision, a closing hymn, and the formula worked so well at scale that it hardened into the only shape a sermon was allowed to take. By the time I came up in the church, the shape was invisible to the people inside it, the way water is invisible to a fish. We did not choose to make the gospel familiar. We inherited a machine for making it familiar, and we kept feeding it, Sunday after Sunday, because it ran and because Saturday was short and because no one in the building could remember the bread tasting like anything else.

So the reversal is sharper than it first appears. The familiar listener is not the obstacle to good preaching. The familiar listener is the judgment on bad preaching. When people have heard it all, they are telling you that you have only ever given them the all they could hear coming. They are a mirror. I have looked into that mirror and not liked the preacher staring back, the man who reached for the predictable phrase because it was Saturday night and the predictable phrase was paid for already.

How then do you preach to such people. You go underneath the summary to the strangeness that the summary was built to manage. Every passage they have heard a hundred times was once scandalous, and the scandal is still in there, buried under our domestications. The prodigal's father did not merely forgive. He ran, and in that culture a grown man did not run, because running meant lifting the robe and showing the legs, and the father took the shame of the boy onto his own body before the boy could say a word (Luke 15:20 ESV). Tell it that way and the woman who has heard the prodigal forty times leans forward, because she has never been allowed to see the father's legs. The information was always there. We sanded it smooth.

It costs more to preach this way, and the cost is the reason most of us do not. To recover the strangeness of a text you have to sit in it long enough to be surprised yourself, and being surprised by a passage you have preached four times requires admitting you did not exhaust it the first three. That admission is a small death. It is far easier to retrieve last year's outline, which already knew where it was going, than to stand again in front of the burning bush and take the sandals off a second time. I have chosen the outline. I have chosen it on a Friday when the week had been cruel and the text felt like a stranger and the old notes were warm and waiting. The people could tell. They always can. A reheated sermon has a particular smell, and the room learns it, and the room stops coming hungry because it has learned what is on the stove.

This is why the cross has to do its work inside the room and not above it. The man who has heard the gospel his whole life is not in danger of forgetting that Christ died. He is in danger of remembering it the way he remembers his own phone number, a true fact that costs nothing to recall. The law has to come first and find him where he actually lives, in the specific contempt he feels for his brother, in the money he will not let go, in the apology he has rehearsed and never given. Grace that answers no particular guilt is grace in the abstract, and the over-familiar have made their peace with grace in the abstract. They have not made their peace with grace for that, named, on a Tuesday. Haddon Robinson insisted that the sermon's idea must press on the actual lives in front of you, not on people in general (Robinson 1980). General grace is the most familiar thing in the room. Particular grace is news.

So do not aim to tell them something they have never heard. Aim to make them feel what they have always known. The woman in the fourth pew is not waiting for a fact. She is waiting to be found. The Word is sharper than any two-edged sword, and it has not gone dull. We have.

Preach the strangeness back into the familiar.

### Works Cited

Brooks, Phillips. 1877. Lectures on Preaching. New York: E. P. Dutton.

Craddock, Fred B. 1971. As One Without Authority. Nashville: Abingdon Press.

Robinson, Haddon W. 1980. Biblical Preaching. Grand Rapids: Baker.

chapters.title: How to Revitalize a Dying Church
chapters.summary: Revitalization is not a program you install but a death the pastor must enter before the congregation can live.
chapters.body:
The numbers came to me on a Tuesday. Average attendance down a third over four years, the giving following it like a shadow, three funerals and no baptisms, and a roof that would not last another Michigan winter. I had the spreadsheet open on the kitchen table when one of my sons asked what was wrong, and I could not answer him, because the honest answer was that I did not know how to make a dying thing live. That is where every revitalization actually begins. Not with a plan. With a man who has run out of plans.

We reach for the wrong question first. We ask how to grow the church, as if growth were the disease working backward, as if the absence of people were the whole of the sickness. But a church can grow numerically and be dead, and a church can shrink and be more alive than it has been in twenty years. The real question is not how to reverse the decline. The real question is whether the body in front of us still wants to be a church at all, or whether it wants to be a club with a steeple, a place where the familiar faces gather to manage their own slow ending with dignity. You cannot answer that question with a survey. You answer it by preaching the gospel and watching who flinches.

There is a strong case against pastors like me even using the word revitalization, and it deserves to be heard at full strength. The critics say that most revitalization talk is church-growth machinery in vestments, that we have taken the language of the New Testament and welded it to attendance metrics borrowed from retail, and that the result is a generation of pastors who measure the Spirit by the parking lot. They are right about more than we would like. Eugene Peterson spent a career warning that the pastoral vocation had been colonized by the shopkeeper's mentality, that we had become managers of religious consumers, fussing over the displays (Peterson 1993, 1). When the critics say our revitalization is often just a more spiritual word for marketing, they have caught us. So let me answer the strongest version of the charge, not the weak one. The strong version is this. A church is not a business and cannot be saved by business means, because its life was never its own to begin with. That is true. And it is precisely why revitalization is possible. A thing that lives by its own strength dies when that strength runs out. A thing that lives by resurrection has a future its accountants cannot see.

Which is why I keep returning to one text, the one I cannot preach without my voice catching. The prophet is set down in the middle of a valley, and the valley is full of bones, and the bones are very many and they are very dry (Ezekiel 37:2 ESV). This is not a church with a budget problem. This is a graveyard with no expectation of a morning. And the Lord asks Ezekiel the only question that matters in a dying church. Son of man, can these bones live. Notice that God does not ask whether Ezekiel can make them live. He asks whether Ezekiel believes they can. And Ezekiel, who is wiser than every consultant I have ever hired, refuses to lie in either direction. He will not say yes, because the evidence is bone-dry against him. He will not say no, because he has met this God before. O Lord God, you know (Ezekiel 37:3 ESV). That is the posture revitalization requires. Not optimism. Not despair. Surrender of the verdict to the only One who has ever raised anything.

We forget how we got here, and the forgetting keeps us reaching for shallow cures. The decline of the inherited church in the West is not a failure of one denomination or one decade. Lesslie Newbigin came home to England in 1974 after thirty-eight years as a missionary in India and found a country that had become, in his words, a pagan society whose public life was governed by assumptions no longer Christian, and harder to reach than any non-Christian culture he had served abroad (Newbigin 1986, 20). He saw what most pastors still refuse to see. The dying church is not a patient with a treatable infection. It is the visible edge of a civilization that quietly relocated its faith from the church to the self somewhere between the Enlightenment and the shopping mall. Charles Taylor traced the architecture of it, the long migration from a world where belief was effortless to a world where belief is one option among many and not the easiest one (Taylor 2007, 3). If you do not see the size of the problem, you will treat a five-hundred-year shift with a six-week sermon series, and you will fail, and you will blame the people in the pews who are simply the last to feel the cold.

So what do we actually do. Here is the reversal that took me years to accept. The pastor does not revitalize the church. The pastor is the first one who has to die. I came into a struggling congregation convinced my energy was the cure, that if I prayed harder and worked longer and programmed smarter the bones would rattle. What I learned is that my frantic competence was part of the death. I was offering them a healthier version of self-reliance, and a church cannot be saved from self-reliance by a more spiritual self-reliance. The dry bones do not come together because the prophet is impressive. They come together because the prophet speaks a word he did not invent over a situation he cannot fix, and then waits for a wind he cannot summon. Prophesy to the breath, the Lord says, and Ezekiel does, and the breath comes (Ezekiel 37:9 ESV). The pastor's whole authority in revitalization is the authority of a man with nothing in his hands but a borrowed word.

This is where the cross does its work, and it does it on the leader before it does it on the congregation. The law comes first, and the law in a dying church is brutal in its honesty. It says your decline is not merely demographic. It says you have loved your own comfort more than the lost neighbor, that you have made the sanctuary a museum of your own memories, that the empty pews are partly the fruit of doors you were happy to keep shut. I have to preach that to myself before I preach it to anyone, because I have done it. I have protected my own schedule from the very people Christ died to reach. The law leaves us in the valley with the bones, and that is exactly where it is supposed to leave us, because grace cannot raise a church that still believes it is only sleeping. Only when we have agreed with God that we are dead can the next sentence land. And you shall know that I am the Lord, when I open your graves (Ezekiel 37:13 ESV). Not when you fix your graves. When I open them.

The practical work follows from this and never precedes it. You will need to preach the whole counsel of God again, not management wisdom in a clerical collar. You will need to know the names and the wounds of the people actually in the room, because Newbigin was right that the only hermeneutic of the gospel a watching world will accept is a congregation that believes it (Newbigin 1989, 227). You will need to raise up others rather than hoard the work, to be patient across years rather than quarters, to bury programs that died long ago and stop holding their funerals every Sunday. None of that is the source of the life. All of it is the riverbed the life runs through when it comes.

My congregation is not what it was. Some of that is grace I can point to, baptisms I did not expect, a young family in the third pew who found Christ from outside everything. Some of it is still bone and still dry, and I have made my peace with not knowing the ending. The question God asked Ezekiel He has never once let me answer with statistics. He asks it of every pastor standing in a valley with a spreadsheet and a roof that will not last the winter. Can these bones live. The only faithful answer is the prophet's answer, the answer that refuses both the lie of optimism and the lie of despair. O Lord God, you know. Then we open our mouths, and we speak the word we did not write, and we wait for a wind that has raised the dead before.

The church is not yours to save. It never was.

### Works Cited

Newbigin, Lesslie. 1986. Foolishness to the Greeks: The Gospel and Western Culture. Grand Rapids: Eerdmans.

Newbigin, Lesslie. 1989. The Gospel in a Pluralist Society. Grand Rapids: Eerdmans.

Peterson, Eugene H. 1993. The Contemplative Pastor: Returning to the Art of Spiritual Direction. Grand Rapids: Eerdmans.

Taylor, Charles. 2007. A Secular Age. Cambridge: Harvard University Press.

chapters.title: Leading a Church When Trust Is Gone
chapters.summary: Trust cannot be restored by competence or charisma but only by the slow, costly work of a leader who tells the truth when the truth indicts him.
chapters.body:
I followed a man who had lied to the congregation for years. Not about money, which would have been simpler, but about who he was, a pattern of deception that came apart all at once and left a church of good people unable to believe anything said from the pulpit, including the things that were true. I arrived eight months after he left. The wound was not in the budget. It was in the eyes. People listened to me preach with their arms folded, not because they disliked me but because the last man had stood in the same spot and sounded sincere, and look what that was worth. You cannot lead people who have learned that listening is dangerous. And they had learned it from a master.

The instinct in that situation is to rebuild trust by being trustworthy, by being competent and consistent and clearly not the last guy, and that instinct is not wrong but it is not nearly enough. The real question when trust is gone is not how the leader proves himself. The real question is whether the leader understands that broken trust is not primarily a problem to be solved but a wound to be grieved, and that the people are not being difficult, they are being faithful to an injury they did not ask for. A pastor who treats lost trust as an obstacle to his leadership has already revealed that he does not understand it. The lost trust is not in his way. It is the thing he is there to serve.

Here is the strongest case against my whole approach, and it comes from sharp people who have watched too many churches paper over real harm. They will say that talk of rebuilding trust is often a tool of institutional self-protection, that when leaders call for unity and healing they usually mean be quiet and let us move on, and that the demand for renewed trust frequently falls hardest on the very people who were hurt, asking the wounded to extend something to the institution that wounded them. This is not cynicism. It is observation, and it is frequently correct. The history of the church's handling of abuse and deception is a history of premature calls for reconciliation that served the powerful and silenced the harmed. I have to grant this in full, because to wave it away would be to commit the exact sin it names. So the honest version of the objection is this. Trust language is often a weapon against the wounded. And the only answer that is not itself a dodge is to insist that real trust can never be rebuilt by asking the hurt to pretend. It can only be rebuilt by leaders willing to stand inside the indictment rather than above it.

The text I carry into these churches is the most uncomfortable restoration scene in the New Testament. Peter had denied Christ three times, publicly, by a fire, when it cost something to be loyal. And the risen Jesus does not restore him with a warm word and a clean slate. By a charcoal fire, the same kind of fire Peter stood at when he lied, Jesus asks him three times, once for each denial, do you love me (John 21:15 ESV). It is not gentle. The text says Peter was grieved because he asked him the third time (John 21:17 ESV). Jesus rebuilds trust by walking Peter straight back into the smell of his own failure and refusing to let him skip past it. This is the pattern, and it is the opposite of how we usually do it. We rebuild trust by changing the subject. Christ rebuilds it by returning to the wound, naming it fully, and only then speaking the future. Feed my sheep. The commission comes after the fire, never instead of it.

The history of this in the church is long and not flattering, and naming it is part of the repair. The crises of trust that have hollowed out congregations across the last several decades, the financial scandals, the abuse coverups, the celebrity pastors whose private lives contradicted every public word, did not erode trust by accident. They eroded it through a consistent institutional reflex to protect the name over the truth, exactly the Sardis reflex, reputation kept alive after integrity had died. Gallup has measured public confidence in American institutions since the early nineteen seventies, and the long line for nearly every institution, the church among them, bends downward across the decades that follow, and the church accelerated its own fall every time it chose the cover story over confession (Gallup 2022).
