We were not merely victims of a cynical age. We taught a watching world to distrust us, one cover-up at a time, and the young especially have learned the lesson well.

Now the reversal, the thing that took me three years in that wounded church to learn. The leader cannot rebuild trust by being trusted. He rebuilds it by being trustworthy in a way that does not depend on whether anyone trusts him yet, and that means his faithfulness has to be aimed past the congregation's approval entirely. The moment I needed their trust in order to lead, I made my leadership a transaction, and they could smell the need, and the need is exactly what the last man had. He needed their belief and so he managed his image to secure it. The only way I could be different was to stop needing their trust and start simply telling the truth, including the truths that cost me, including the times I was wrong in front of them, with no anxious eye on whether it was working. Trust, it turns out, is never built by the man who is trying to build it. It is the slow accidental fruit of a man who has stopped trying and started confessing. Eugene Peterson said that the pastor's integrity is in the unseen disciplines, the angles no congregation watches, and that a ministry built for the visible approval rots at the unseen root (Peterson 1987, 2).

So the law comes, and it comes for the leader before it comes for the people who broke trust. The law says that a pastor inheriting a wounded church will be tempted to use the wound, to position himself as the trustworthy rescuer against the villain who left, and that this self-positioning is its own quiet lie. I have done it. I have let a congregation's relief at my arrival become a thing I enjoyed too much, have let myself be the hero of a story whose real hero is Christ and whose real victims deserved more lament than I gave them. The law indicts the rescuer fantasy. It says that the man who rebuilds trust by being the not-villain is still making the church about himself, just in a more flattering pose. I cannot stand outside this. I am exactly the kind of leader who would rather be admired for honesty than actually pay its cost.

And then grace, which is the only ground a wounded church can finally stand on. The grace is that the trust the congregation most needs to recover is not trust in their leaders, who will fail them again because all leaders are men, but trust in the Christ who restored Peter at the fire and did not flinch from the wound. A church whose trust in its pastors has been destroyed has, painfully, been freed from an idol it should never have had. It was never safe to put ultimate trust in a man. The collapse of that trust, brutal as it is, can become the doorway to a deeper and unbreakable trust in the only One who has never once managed His image, who told the truth about us at the cost of His life, and who returns to our fires not to shame us but to commission us. Feed my sheep is spoken to a man who failed and was not pretended past it. That is the only kind of leader a broken church can follow. One who knows the fire.

Trust does not come back when the leader proves he is worthy. It comes back, slowly, when the leader stops needing it and starts telling the truth, especially the truth that costs him. There is no shortcut. There was none for Peter. There is none for me.

The fire is where it starts. We would rather it started anywhere else.

### Works Cited

Gallup. 2022. Confidence in U.S. Institutions Down to a New Low Average. Washington, DC: Gallup.

Peterson, Eugene H. 1987. Working the Angles: The Shape of Pastoral Integrity. Grand Rapids: Eerdmans.

chapters.title: Leading Through Conflict on a Church Team
chapters.summary: A church team does not get into trouble because it fights, it gets into trouble because it learned to call avoidance peace.
chapters.body:
Two staff members have not directly spoken to each other in four months, and everyone knows it, and nobody says it. They are professionals. They pass each other in the hall. They sit on the same row in the all-staff meeting and route every actual message through a third person who has become an unwilling diplomat between two people who used to be friends. The team is functioning. The calendar fills, the services happen, the bulletin gets printed. And underneath the function a low current of avoidance is running through everything, and the longer it runs the more the whole team organizes itself around not setting it off.

We have a strange relationship with conflict in the church. We treat it as a failure of sanctification, as if a mature team would simply never disagree, as if the presence of friction proves the absence of the Spirit. So when conflict shows up, and it always shows up, we feel ashamed of it and we hide it. We swallow the disagreement and call the swallowing humility. We let the resentment build and call the building patience. And the conflict does not go anywhere. It just moves down, out of the meeting and into the body, into the headaches and the clipped emails and the Sunday smiles that do not reach the eyes.

Let me steel-man the peacemaker, because he is quoting Jesus and he is not wrong about much. Blessed are the peacemakers. A quarrelsome church is a poor witness, and the world is watching how we treat each other, and Paul begged the Philippians to be of the same mind. The peacemaker has seen what unchecked conflict does, has watched a church split over a building program and never recover, has buried friendships that died in a business meeting. His instinct to protect the unity of the team is not cowardice. It is the scar tissue of someone who has seen the alternative. He is guarding something he has watched bleed out before.

But he has misread the text he is standing on, and the misreading is costing him the very thing he wants. Peacemaking is not peacekeeping. The peacemaker in the Sermon on the Mount is an active figure who goes into the broken place and makes something, the way a steelworker makes a beam, through heat and pressure and joining. The peacekeeper is a different creature entirely. He keeps the peace by keeping the lid on, and the lid is not peace, it is a delay. What he calls unity is two people not speaking for four months while a third carries their mail. Jesus did not bless that. He blessed the harder and braver thing, the one that walks into the conflict on purpose and stays until something is actually mended.

The spine text is plainer than we admit, and it is from Jesus' own mouth. 'If your brother sins against you, go and tell him his fault, between you and him alone' (Matthew 18:15 ESV). Go. The movement is toward the person, not away. Alone, which means not to the third party, not to the prayer chain disguised as concern, not to the spouse over dinner, not to the loose coalition you are quietly building in the hallway. The most disobeyed verse in church staff life is not about money or sex or doctrine. It is this one, the simple command to take the problem to the person and nobody else, and our entire architecture of avoidance exists to get around it.

Watch what triangulation actually does to a team, because it is the disease underneath most church conflict. Edwin Friedman built his whole understanding of congregations on the way anxiety moves through relationships, and he showed that when two people cannot tolerate the tension between them, they will reliably pull in a third to stabilize it (Friedman 2007). The third person feels useful, even chosen, carrying messages and absorbing complaints. But the triangle does not resolve the conflict. It preserves it. It lets two people stay angry indefinitely because the pressure that would have forced them to deal with each other is being bled off through someone else. Every staff has these triangles. Most pastors are sitting inside several of them and feeling needed instead of feeling alarmed.

We did not invent this avoidance. We inherited it, and the history clarifies the grip it has. The therapeutic turn in American culture, which the sociologist Philip Rieff diagnosed as early as nineteen sixty-six in his account of the triumph of the therapeutic, taught us to read every relational difficulty as a matter of feelings to be managed and validated rather than truths to be told (Rieff 1966). The church drank deeply from that stream. We learned to prize emotional comfort above honest correction, to fear hurting someone more than we feared leaving them in sin, to mistake niceness for love. A whole generation of church teams now treats the avoidance of hard words as the highest relational virtue, and we cannot find the verse that taught us that, because there is no such verse.

Here is the reversal. The conflict you are avoiding is not the threat to the team. The avoidance is the threat. Lencioni mapped this with uncomfortable precision when he showed that teams which cannot engage in honest conflict do not become more unified, they become less committed, because people will not buy into a decision they were never allowed to argue with (Lencioni 2002). The silence you are protecting is producing the disengagement you are about to complain about. The meeting where nobody pushes back is not a sign of alignment. It is the sound of people who have stopped believing their voice changes anything, saving their real opinions for the parking lot where the decisions get quietly unmade.

So lead into it. When you sense the four-month silence, name it out loud and decline to be the third corner of the triangle, sending the two people back to each other with your blessing and your expectation. When someone comes to complain about a colleague, the most pastoral question you can ask is whether they have said this to the person directly, and the most pastoral answer to no is to walk with them until they do. Set the table so that conflict in the meeting is normal and conflict in the hallway is not. The team that fights well in the open is the team that does not need to fight in the dark.

And remember that the alternative to honest conflict is not peace but a burden no single person can carry. In the wilderness Moses came apart under exactly this weight. The people quarreled and complained and routed every grievance through him, and he cried out to God that he was not able to carry all this people alone, that the load was too heavy, that he would rather die than keep bearing it by himself (Numbers 11:14 ESV). The Lord's answer was not to make the conflict disappear. It was to spread the weight, to take of the Spirit on Moses and put it on seventy elders so that they would bear the burden of the people with him and Moses would not bear it alone (Numbers 11:17 ESV). Read what God refuses to do. He does not promise Moses a quiet camp. He gives him shared leadership, a body of people willing to stand inside the tension with him rather than route it around him. The leader who absorbs every conflict alone, who lets himself become the third corner of every triangle, is not being strong. He is doing the very thing God told Moses to stop doing, and it will crush him the same way. Nouwen called the alternative the downward movement of Christian leadership, the refusal to escape conflict through power, the choice to remain present and bear the weight together where it would be easier to dominate or disappear (Nouwen 1989).

I have to name my own part in this, because I led a team for years that I was proud of for never fighting, and I have since come to understand that I was proud of the wrong thing. The reason nobody fought in my meetings was not that we had achieved some rare maturity. It was that I had made disagreement expensive, in a hundred small ways I never noticed, and my people had done the arithmetic and decided silence was cheaper. The peace I prized was the peace of a room that had given up on changing my mind. It took a staff member leaving, and telling me on the way out the things she had never felt safe to say while she stayed, before I understood that the quiet I had treated as a trophy was actually the bill coming due. I had mistaken the absence of conflict for the presence of unity, and the two had never been further apart.

A team that has learned to fight honestly and stay is more unified than a team that has never fought at all, the way a bone that healed is stronger than a bone that was never tested. We keep protecting our teams from the one thing that would actually bind them together. We keep choosing the quiet, and the quiet keeps costing us the thing the quiet was supposed to save.

Peace is not the absence of conflict. It is conflict carried all the way through.

### Works Cited

Friedman, Edwin H. 2007. A Failure of Nerve: Leadership in the Age of the Quick Fix. New York: Seabury Books.

Lencioni, Patrick. 2002. The Five Dysfunctions of a Team. San Francisco: Jossey-Bass.

Nouwen, Henri J. M. 1989. In the Name of Jesus: Reflections on Christian Leadership. New York: Crossroad.

Rieff, Philip. 1966. The Triumph of the Therapeutic: Uses of Faith After Freud. New York: Harper and Row.

chapters.title: Preaching Politics Without Losing the Gospel
chapters.summary: The choice is not between a political pulpit and a pure one, because silence is already a politics, and the only question is whether the cross or the party is doing the ruling.
chapters.body:
It is the second Sunday of November and the preacher has a decision to make before he opens his mouth. Half the room voted one way. Half voted the other. Both halves are watching his eyes for a sign. He could mention nothing, and the half that wanted him to speak will hear cowardice. He could mention something, and the other half will hear betrayal. He stands there with a text in his hand and a country in his pews, and there is no neutral sentence available to him. Even the weather report would be heard as a verdict.

This is the bind, and pretending it does not exist is the first failure. Karl Barth is widely paraphrased as telling young preachers to take the Bible in one hand and the newspaper in the other, and that compressed line gets quoted as permission to politicize everything. What he actually said, in a 1963 interview, was harder. Take your Bible and take your newspaper, he told them, and read both, but interpret the newspaper from your Bible and never once the Bible from the newspaper (Barth 1963). The moment the newspaper starts editing the Bible, you no longer have a preacher. You have a chaplain to a faction, blessing what the faction already decided to do.

The strongest argument for keeping politics out of the pulpit is not cowardice, and it is dishonest to treat it as such. It runs like this. The church gathers people who disagree about tax policy and immigration and war, and it gathers them around a table that those disagreements cannot reach. When the preacher takes a side on the contested questions of the hour, he fences off the table. He tells the brother who voted differently that he is welcome to commune but not to belong. Worse, he binds the eternal gospel to a platform that will look foolish in twenty years, and when the platform falls the gospel is dragged down with it. Keep the pulpit clean, this argument says, so that the one thing the world cannot hear anywhere else stays audible. I find this argument serious. I have used it. There were Sundays I used it to protect myself, and called the protection wisdom.

But take it at its strongest and it still fails at one point, and the point is decisive. The argument assumes there is a category called politics that sits outside the gospel, a separate room the preacher can choose to enter or avoid. There is no such room. When Scripture says that the Lord executes justice for the oppressed and gives food to the hungry (Psalm 146:7 ESV), it has already entered the room the argument wanted to keep sealed. The question of whether the hungry eat is not adjacent to the gospel. It is downstream of the character of God. To refuse to speak it is not neutrality. It is a vote for the way things are, cast by a man who has convinced himself that not voting is an option.

Carry the prophet Amos as the spine, because Amos is where this gets tested. He was a herdsman from Tekoa, not a court preacher, and around the year 760 before Christ he walked north into the prosperous kingdom of Israel under Jeroboam the Second and said the most political thing imaginable. He named the economics by name. They sell the righteous for silver and the needy for a pair of sandals (Amos 2:6 ESV). He named the women of the comfortable class as cows of Bashan who crush the needy and tell their husbands to bring drinks (Amos 4:1 ESV). This is not gentle. This is a man pointing at the policy of a nation and the dinner habits of its donors. And the priest Amaziah did exactly what the keep-it-clean argument would have him do. He told Amos to take his preaching back south, to earn his bread somewhere else, because the sanctuary at Bethel was the king's, a temple of the kingdom (Amos 7:13 ESV).

The timing of Amos matters, and it indicts us, because Jeroboam's reign was a boom. The borders were wide, the markets were full, the festivals were crowded, and the worship was, by every external measure, thriving. This is the detail we skip. Amos did not preach into a collapsing nation begging for a word. He preached into a confident, religious, prosperous one, a nation whose churches were full and whose conscience was asleep, and the thing the Lord could not stomach was precisely the worship. I hate, I despise your feasts, he says, and takes no delight in your solemn assemblies (Amos 5:21 ESV). The singing offended God because the singing covered the selling of the needy. That is the political sermon at its sharpest, the one that walks into the largest, happiest congregation in the land and says the songs are an offense because of what the singers do on Monday. No preacher gives that sermon by accident, and no preacher gives it to stay popular.

There it is, the whole problem in one sentence from a priest. Bethel was the king's sanctuary. Amaziah had made the pulpit an arm of the palace, and so the only politics he could not hear was the politics of God. He thought he was keeping religion out of politics. He had it exactly backward. He had let politics swallow the religion so completely that the word of the Lord sounded to him like sedition. This is the warning for every preacher who imagines that silence keeps him clean. Silence has an owner. At Bethel the owner was the king.

So the danger runs in both directions, and honesty requires naming the second one as plainly as the first. The man who preaches the party from the pulpit has lost the gospel just as surely as Amaziah lost it, only from the opposite door. He has taken the cross, which judges every kingdom, and he has stapled it to one kingdom and called the staple faithfulness. John Stott described preaching as bridge-building between the ancient text and the modern world, and he warned that a bridge anchored only on the modern bank is no bridge at all, just a ramp into the prejudices of the age (Stott 1982). The party preacher has built a ramp. He flatters the half of the room that already agreed with him and calls their agreement revival.

Here is the line that holds, and it is the line of the cross itself. The cross is political, because it was a political execution carried out by an empire on a man it considered a threat to public order. But the cross is political in a way that no party can survive. It indicts the religious leaders who handed him over and the imperial governor who washed his hands and the crowd that chose Barabbas, and it leaves no faction standing as the hero. When you preach the cross with its full weight, you do not take a side in the room's argument. You announce a judgment that falls on both sides and a mercy offered to both. That is harder than partisanship and harder than silence, because both halves will be uncomfortable, and the preacher will not get the warm thing that comes from telling people they are right.

Law before grace, and here the law has to find the actual idol. For one half of the room the idol is order, the fear that the country is slipping and only power can hold it. For the other half the idol is progress, the certainty that history is theirs and the resisters are obstacles. The preacher who only ever convicts one of these idols has been captured by the other. I have stood in front of a room and known exactly which idol I was willing to name and which one I would let sleep, and the one I let sleep was always the one my own heart was guarding. The newspaper had gotten into my Bible after all.

There is a test for whether you have preached politics or preached the party, and it is brutal in its simplicity. After the sermon, which half of the room felt comforted. If the same half walks out warmed every single week, the half that already agreed with you on Friday, then you have not been preaching the cross. You have been preaching the platform, and the cross has become the decoration on the platform. The genuinely prophetic word leaves your own side uneasy too, because the kingdom of God does not map onto any ballot, and the man who has heard it rightly goes home unable to feel fully at home in the camp he arrived in. I came to faith out of atheism, which means I have no inherited tribe in the church to protect, and I still catch myself protecting one, the one I drifted into, the one whose approval feels like belonging. The pull is not theological. It is the simple hunger to be on a side that will have me, and that hunger has bent more sermons than bad exegesis ever did.

So preach the issue when the text raises it, and let the text decide which issue and which week, not the news cycle, not the donor, not the half of the room you are afraid of. Brueggemann argued that the prophetic word does its work not by scolding but by offering a counter-world so vivid that the official world loses its grip (Brueggemann 1989). That is the aim. Not to tell people how to vote. To make the kingdom of God so concrete in their imagination that every kingdom of this world, including the one they voted for, looks smaller than it did on Tuesday.

You will lose people either way. Lose them to the gospel, not to the party.

### Works Cited

Barth, Karl. 1963. Barth in Retirement. Interview. Time, May 31, 1963.

Brueggemann, Walter. 1989. Finally Comes the Poet. Minneapolis: Fortress Press.

Stott, John R. W. 1982. Between Two Worlds. Grand Rapids: Eerdmans.

chapters.title: Replanting: When a Church Has to Start Over
chapters.summary: Replanting asks a congregation to do the one thing flesh resists most, to lay down its own life so that something it will not control can rise in its place.
chapters.body:
The vote was twenty-three to nine. Twenty-three older members of a congregation that had run six hundred strong in 1978 agreed to dissolve as they were and hand their building, their name, their endowment, and their Sunday morning to a replant they would not lead and could barely recognize. I was in the room as an outside voice, and I watched a woman in her eighties raise her hand for yes with tears running down her face. Afterward I asked her how she could vote to end the church she had given her life to. She said it was the only way to keep it from ending. Then she said something I have not been able to shake. We are not voting to die. We are voting to be buried, which is different, because you only bury what you expect to see again.

Replanting is the hardest word in this whole vocabulary, harder than revitalization, because revitalization still lets a church believe it is fundamentally the same body getting healthier. Replanting does not. Replanting says this body, as it is, cannot continue, and that the most faithful thing it can do is hand its life to a new work that will keep very little of what it was. The real question in a replant is not strategic. It is spiritual to the bone. Can a congregation love Christ and His mission more than it loves its own continuation. Almost everything else is logistics. That one question is the whole war.

Let me steel-man the people who say no, because they are not villains and the easy caricature of them is a lie. The members who resist a replant are usually accused of selfishness, of clinging to the carpet and the casseroles. But the strongest version of their position is not selfish at all. They will say that a church is not an interchangeable franchise, that it is a particular people with a particular history, that the saints buried in its memory and the prayers prayed in its walls are not disposable, and that to wipe it all away and call the result the same church is a kind of forgery. There is real theological weight here. The communion of saints is not a brand to be relaunched. Tim Keller, who spent his career thinking about how churches start and renew, warned against treating congregations as mere delivery systems for programs, insisting that a church is a body with a history and a culture that cannot be engineered from a manual (Keller 2012, 19). So the honest version of the objection is this. Replanting risks treating a living tradition as scrap. And the answer to that objection is not to deny it but to go through it, because Scripture has a category for a death that honors what died precisely by refusing to embalm it.

The spine here is the same hard saying of Jesus that haunts every page of this subject. Truly, truly, I say to you, unless a grain of wheat falls into the earth and dies, it remains alone, but if it dies, it bears much fruit (John 12:24 ESV). Notice what the seed keeps and what it loses. It does not keep its shape. The husk is destroyed, dissolved in the dark, unrecognizable. But the seed keeps its life, its very specific genetic identity, and what rises is not a different plant but the same life in a form the seed could never have produced by staying intact. This is the exact answer to the objection. Replanting done faithfully is not the erasure of a tradition. It is the burial of a husk so that the life inside it can rise. The woman in her eighties understood the verse better than the consultants. You only bury what you expect to see again.

The history of this is older and more Protestant than we admit. We talk about replanting as a new movement of the last fifteen years, and the practical models are recent, but the underlying conviction runs back to the Reformation itself, which was at bottom a massive replant. The reformers did not believe they were inventing a new church. They believed they were recovering a buried one, that the institution had so encrusted the gospel that the only faithful move was to tear down structures and start the visible church again on the recovered foundation. Mark Noll has shown how the renewal movements that shaped Protestant vitality across the centuries came again and again through disruption rather than maintenance, through people willing to lose the existing form to recover the buried center (Noll 1992, 4). Replanting is not a betrayal of the inherited church. It is the inherited church doing the very thing it was born doing.

Now the reversal, and it is the one that converts a strategy into a death worth dying. We assume the replant is for the sake of the new people, the unreached neighborhood, the young families who will fill the rebuilt sanctuary. That is true but it is not the deepest truth. The replant is also, and maybe first, for the sake of the people voting yes. Because the act of laying down your own church for a future you will not control is itself the most Christlike thing many of those saints will ever do, and it forms them in the image of their Lord more than another decade of survival ever could. I have watched older believers come spiritually alive in the very act of agreeing to their congregation's death, freed at last from the exhausting work of keeping a dying thing propped up, released into the joy of pure gift. The replant did not just serve the new. It saved the old from the slow corrosion of self-preservation. Eugene Peterson said the pastoral task is to keep insisting that the most important things are the things we cannot make happen, only receive (Peterson 1987, 6). The yes vote is exactly that, a refusal to make survival happen, an opening of the hands.

The law has to be preached here without flinching, and it cuts the leader first. The law says that much of our resistance to replanting is idolatry wearing the mask of faithfulness. We say we are protecting the legacy, and sometimes we are protecting our own importance, our own grief, our own fear of admitting that what we built could not last. I have felt this in myself. I have wanted a thing I led to outlive me more than I have wanted Christ to be honored in its ending, and that wanting is not love, it is the same self-preservation the gospel came to kill. The law strips the noble language off the fear and shows it for what it is. A church that will not die for the mission has already started worshiping itself, and the slow death that follows is not tragedy. It is judgment.

And then grace, which is the only thing that makes the burial bearable. The grace is that the God who asks the seed to fall into the earth is the same God who went into the earth first. Christ did not ask of any congregation a death He had not already died, alone, in the dark, with no guarantee visible to flesh that anything would rise. And because He rose, the burial of a faithful church is not a leap into nothing. It is a leap into the pattern of the only One who has ever come back from where He went. The endowment becomes seed. The building becomes soil. The saints who voted yes become, in their final ministry, the very wheat their Lord described, and what rises in that place will carry their life in a form they could not have imagined and will, I believe, one day recognize.

Not every church should be replanted. Some have the health to be revitalized and should be. Some are too far gone for either and should be buried with honor and no pretense of resurrection in this age. Discernment is the whole art, and it cannot be reduced to a flowchart. But where a replant is the faithful road, the church that takes it is not surrendering. It is doing the most ancient Christian thing there is. It is following its Lord into the ground, in the stubborn confidence that the ground is not the end of the story but the one place the story has always begun.

You only bury what you expect to see again. The saints knew that before the consultants did.

### Works Cited

Keller, Timothy. 2012. Center Church: Doing Balanced, Gospel-Centered Ministry in Your City. Grand Rapids: Zondervan.

Noll, Mark A. 1992. A History of Christianity in the United States and Canada. Grand Rapids: Eerdmans.

Peterson, Eugene H. 1987. Working the Angles: The Shape of Pastoral Integrity. Grand Rapids: Eerdmans.

chapters.title: The Difference Between a Sermon and a Talk
chapters.summary: A talk informs you and lets you go, but a sermon claims you, and the difference is not the subject or the skill but who is doing the speaking through the man.
chapters.body:
A man stands up with notes and speaks for thirty minutes about God, and at the end you cannot tell whether what just happened was a sermon or a talk. The room cannot tell either. They clap or they do not, they take notes or they do not, and they go home essentially unchanged, having heard something true and useful and survivable. That last word is the whole problem. A talk is survivable. You can hear a good talk and remain exactly who you were. The question of what makes a good sermon is, at bottom, the question of why a sermon is not supposed to be survivable.

The two can look identical from the back row. Both can have a clear point and a memorable line and an honest delivery. Both can quote Scripture. Both can be moving. The difference is not visible in the technique, which is why so much preaching instruction misses it, drilling the mechanics of a thing whose essence is not mechanical. You can teach a man everything about how to give a talk and have taught him nothing about how to preach, because you have trained the hands and never touched the question of who is speaking.

Let me build the case that there is no real difference, because intelligent people make it and it deserves answering. A sermon, the argument runs, is just a religious talk. It uses a Bible instead of a business case, it ends in prayer instead of applause, but the underlying act is the same, a prepared person communicating ideas to a listening group. The talk that helps a man forgive his father has done more good than a sermon that bored him. Communication is communication, and the spiritual gloss we put on preaching is mostly the profession protecting its mystique. There is a real point buried here, and I will grant it before I answer it. A sermon that is badly communicated is not made holy by being a sermon. Clarity is not optional. Mumbling is not anointing. Many sermons would be improved by learning what a good talk knows.

But take the argument at its strongest, that communication is communication, and it collapses on one verse. Paul reminds the Romans that faith comes from hearing, and hearing through the word of Christ (Romans 10:17 ESV), and then he asks how they will hear without someone preaching, and how anyone will preach unless he is sent (Romans 10:14-15 ESV). That word sent is the whole difference. A talk is something a man decides to give. A sermon is something a man is sent to deliver. The speaker of a talk is the source. The preacher of a sermon is a courier, and a courier who edits the message is a thief. The act is not the same, because the authority behind the act is not the same, and the listener, even one who could not explain it, feels the difference between a man offering his opinion and a man under orders.

Carry that sent-ness as the spine, because it changes everything downstream. Augustine, who had been a professional teacher of rhetoric before his conversion, wrestled with exactly this in the fourth book of his treatise on Christian teaching, written near the year 426. He knew every device of the talk, every trick of persuasion the empire could teach. And he concluded that the Christian speaker must subordinate all of it to a higher aim, that he speaks not to be admired but so that the truth may be loved and obeyed, and that his own life must preach alongside his tongue or the tongue is a clanging thing (Augustine 426). The rhetorician gives a talk to win the room. The preacher, Augustine saw, is trying to lose the room to God. Those are not two grades of the same act. They are opposite acts that happen to use the same lungs.

What makes Augustine's argument matter is that he was not a man suspicious of skill. He had eaten his bread by skill. He had taught young men in Milan how to move a crowd toward whatever the crowd needed to be moved toward, and he never once pretended that eloquence was worthless. He kept it. He told preachers to use the whole armory of the rhetoricians, the clear style for teaching, the moderate style for delight, the grand style for bending the will. But he reversed the master. In the schools, the cause served the eloquence, because a paid speaker would defend any cause that paid. In the church, the eloquence serves the cause, and the cause is fixed, and the speaker did not choose it and may not amend it. That single reversal is the whole boundary line between a talk and a sermon. The talker owns his subject and bends it to his gift. The preacher is owned by his subject and bends his gift to it. A man can have the identical skill in both rooms and be doing two different things, because in one room he is the lord of the message and in the other he is its servant.

This is why the cross has to be in a sermon in a way it never has to be in a talk. A talk about generosity can stand on its own legs, can move a man to write a check by the sheer force of the case. A sermon about generosity that does not run, sooner or later, into the one who though he was rich became poor so that we through his poverty might become rich (2 Corinthians 8:9 ESV), is a talk wearing a stole. The cross is the watershed. A talk persuades you to do better. A sermon announces that you cannot do better, kills the man who thought he could, and raises a new one who gives because he has been given to. The first leaves you with a task. The second leaves you with a grave and a resurrection. Tim Keller pressed this point hard, that preaching to the heart must always show how the text drives to Christ and his work, or it becomes mere moral advice with a religious accent (Keller 2015). Moral advice is a fine talk. It is a failed sermon.

And here is the reversal, the thing that humbles the preacher who thinks he can manufacture the difference. The man cannot make his talk into a sermon by his own effort. He cannot add enough Scripture or enough passion or enough cross to cross the line by technique, because the line is not technical. A sermon happens when God speaks through the speaking, and that is not in the preacher's power to guarantee. He can only prepare the kindling. The fire is given. This should terrify us out of our professionalism and free us from it at the same time, because it means the worst-delivered sermon, given by a sent man who has been broken by his text, may do what the most polished talk can never do, while the preacher who trusts his polish may give a flawless talk every Sunday for thirty years and never once preach.

I know which of those preachers I have most often been, and the confession is not modesty. There were years I gave excellent talks. They were clear, they were warm, they had a line people quoted in the lobby, and they cost me almost nothing, because I had not let the text get its hands on me before I stood up. I had studied the passage the way a lawyer studies a brief, mastering it, standing over it, never once standing under it. A talk is what comes out of a man who has mastered his material. A sermon is what comes out of a man whose material has mastered him, and the difference is felt in the chest before it is understood in the mind. My polished years were my emptiest years. The people were entertained and unchanged, and so was I, and I mistook the lobby compliments for fruit until a season came that broke me open and I learned, late, what it costs to actually be sent.

So what makes a good sermon. Not the skill, though skill serves it. Not the subject, though it must be the right subject. A good sermon is one through which a man who was sent says the thing he was sent to say, having been changed by it first, so that the cross does its killing and its raising work inside the room, and the people leave unable to remain who they were. Phillips Brooks called it truth through personality, and the personality matters, but the truth is the master and the man is the window (Brooks 1877). A talk shows you the man. A sermon shows you through him to the thing that has hold of him.

The test is the morning after. A talk you admired. A sermon admired you back, found you, named you, and would not let you stay. If you remember the speaker, it may have been a fine talk. If you cannot stop thinking about your own life, your father, your money, your unforgiveness, the grave you have been avoiding, it was probably a sermon, and the speaker has already done the one thing a preacher is for. He got out of the way.

A talk you survive. A sermon survives you.

### Works Cited

Augustine. 426. On Christian Teaching. Translated by R. P. H. Green. Oxford: Oxford University Press.

Brooks, Phillips. 1877. Lectures on Preaching. New York: E. P. Dutton.

Keller, Timothy. 2015. Preaching. New York: Viking.

chapters.title: The Interior Life of the Pastor
chapters.summary: A pastor can handle the things of God all week and starve to death spiritually, because handling is not the same as eating.
chapters.body:
There is a particular kind of hunger that only afflicts people who work with food all day. The cook surrounded by meals he never sits down to eat. The pastor surrounded by Scripture he only ever prepares for someone else. I have stood in my study with an open Bible at ten on a Tuesday morning and realized, with a cold clarity, that I had not read a word of it for my own soul in weeks. I had read it for the sermon. I had read it for the funeral. I had not read it for the bread it is. That is a confession, and it is more common among us than we admit.

The interior life is the part of a pastor that no one sees and everything depends on. It is the man as he is when the building is empty, when no one is watching the prayer, when there is no sermon to harvest from the text. And it is precisely because no one sees it that it is the first thing to go. We are paid for the public man. We are evaluated on the public man. The interior man pays no bills and fills no pews, and so he gets fed last, which means in a busy season he does not get fed at all.

Let me grant the strongest objection before I go further, because it has weight. Some will say this whole emphasis on the pastor's inner world is a modern indulgence, a kind of spiritual navel-gazing that the apostles would not have recognized. Paul did not write about his interior life. He planted churches, took beatings, ran hard, and trusted God to sustain him in the running. The fixation on inner experience, the objection goes, is a symptom of a therapeutic age that has turned even prayer into a project of self-improvement, and a pastor would do better to obey God and stop monitoring his own soul like a man taking his temperature every hour.

There is truth there, and I want to honor it. A spirituality that is forever examining itself can curdle into a new kind of self-absorption, and the cure for an anxious pastor is not always more introspection. But the objection misreads its own apostle. Paul wrote that though our outer self is wasting away, our inner self is being renewed day by day (2 Corinthians 4:16 ESV). He had an interior life, and he tended it, and the running he did was fueled by a renewal that happened in the hidden man. The objection also forgets the Lord Himself, who, in the press of a ministry more urgent than any of ours, rose while it was still dark and went out to a desolate place and prayed (Mark 1:35). The most needed man in Israel withdrew from the need to be with His Father. If He required it, the notion that we have outgrown it is not maturity. It is presumption.

So I will carry that text, Mark 1, through this. The scene is exact and it indicts me. Jesus has healed all evening, the whole town gathered at the door, and the next morning, very early, while it is still dark, He gets up and goes off alone to pray. Then the disciples find Him, almost scandalized, and say everyone is looking for you (Mark 1:37). There is the pressure every pastor knows. Everyone is looking for you. The work is waiting. The needs are stacking up at the door. And the Son of God had, the night before, chosen the desolate place over the waiting crowd, not because the crowd did not matter but because He could not be for the crowd what He needed to be without first being alone with the Father. He drew His public ministry out of His hidden communion. We try to run a public ministry on an empty interior, and then wonder at the hollowness in our own preaching.

I come at this as a man who began with no interior life at all that he would have called by that name. I was an atheist. The inner world I had was a closed room with no window toward heaven, and the great surprise of conversion was the window opening. But here is the danger I did not anticipate. A man can be converted and then slowly board that window back up, not with unbelief but with busyness, until the room is once again sealed, and the strange agony of a sealed-up Christian is that he remembers the light and cannot find it. I was raised without a father, and prayer, the practice of being a beloved child before a present Father, was the very muscle I had never developed and most needed. For years I prayed the way a stranger speaks to a landlord. It took a long time to learn to pray the way a son speaks to a father who is glad he came in.

The history of how pastors lost the interior life is partly a history of good intentions. The Protestant recovery of the Word rightly put preaching at the center, but over centuries the pastor's relationship to Scripture quietly shifted from the man who feeds on it to the man who processes it. Ruth Haley Barton describes the way leaders come to relate to spiritual things functionally, using prayer and Scripture as tools for ministry rather than as means of their own communion with God, until they are, in her phrase, leading on empty (Barton 2008). Dallas Willard spent his life arguing that the missing piece in evangelical ministry was a real apprenticeship to Jesus in the actual practices of the inner life, that we had reduced the gospel to a transaction about the afterlife and lost the present reality of life with God (Willard 1998). We trained men to explain the bread. We did not always teach them to eat it.

Here is the reversal. The hidden life is not preparation for the real work. The hidden life is the real work, and the public ministry is its overflow. Eugene Peterson said the three pastoral acts of praying, reading Scripture, and giving spiritual direction are so unobtrusive that they are easy to skip, and yet they are the angles, the unseen lines, that determine whether the visible shape of the ministry is true or distorted (Peterson 1987). Skip the angles, and the visible structure looks fine for a while, then slowly goes crooked, and everyone can see the crookedness but no one can name the cause, because the cause is invisible. The cause is a man who stopped meeting God in private and is now performing a God he no longer knows.

There is a practical objection I should answer before I reach the cross, because busy men will raise it. When. When does a pastor whose week is already full of urgent need find the hours for a hidden life that produces nothing the church can see. I have asked it myself, usually in the tone of a man looking for permission to skip the thing he knows he needs. But notice that the question assumes the interior life is one more task to be fit into a full schedule, and that assumption is the disease. The interior life is not an item on the list. It is the soil out of which everything else on the list either grows healthy or grows sick. A farmer does not ask when he will find time to have soil. The soil is the precondition of the harvest, and the man who neglects it to spend more hours planting is not more diligent, he is farming dust. Jesus rose before dawn not because His calendar had a gap but because His public life was unsustainable without His hidden one, and so is yours, and so is mine.

There is also a quieter reason we avoid the interior life, and it is worth naming because naming it is half the cure. The hidden room is where God deals with us about ourselves, and many of us would rather stay busy than be that exposed. As long as I am preparing a sermon I am safe, I am the one with the answers, I am the handler of the text and not its subject. The moment I sit in the dark before dawn with nothing to prepare and no one to instruct, the text turns and begins to read me, and what it finds is not always flattering. Avoidance of the interior life is often avoidance of self-knowledge before God, and a pastor can hide from his own soul behind the very Scriptures he expounds. I have done it. The flight into busyness can be, underneath, a flight from the God who wants to tell me the truth about myself, and that truth is the doorway to every mercy I most need.

The cross, law first. The law here is sharp. To handle the holy things professionally while not communing with the Holy One personally is the sin of the man who serves at the altar and despises the One the altar is for. It is possible to preach Christ and not know Christ, to be, in the end, a tour guide pointing at a country he has never entered. I have stood closer to that man than I want to say. The grace second. The cross opened the way into the very presence of God, tore the veil from top to bottom, made the holiest place accessible to a man with bloody hands and a divided heart (Matthew 27:51). The invitation to commune is not earned by the quality of your interior life. It is purchased by Christ and offered to you in your emptiness. You do not have to assemble a worthy inner life before you come in. You come in empty, and the coming in is how it fills.

The pastor's most important sermon is the one no one will ever hear, preached in a dark room before dawn, to an audience of One.

Feed the hidden man. The visible one is starving in front of you.

### Works Cited

Barton, Ruth Haley. 2008. Strengthening the Soul of Your Leadership: Seeking God in the Crucible of Ministry. Downers Grove, IL: InterVarsity Press.

Peterson, Eugene H. 1987. Working the Angles: The Shape of Pastoral Integrity. Grand Rapids: Eerdmans.

Willard, Dallas. 1998. The Divine Conspiracy: Rediscovering Our Hidden Life in God. San Francisco: HarperSanFrancisco.

The Holy Bible, English Standard Version. 2001. Wheaton, IL: Crossway.

chapters.title: The Lonely Seat: Power and the Senior Leader
chapters.summary: The loneliness of the senior seat is real, and the way most pastors try to cure it is exactly what makes it worse.
chapters.body:
A pastor stands at the door after the third service, and forty people tell him it was exactly what they needed, and he drives home and cannot think of a single person he could call to say he is not okay. He leads a staff of twelve. He has elders who pray for him by name. He is surrounded all week by people who depend on him, who admire him, who would say without hesitation that they love him. And he is alone in a way that none of them can see, because the seat he sits in has put a pane of glass between him and everyone who reports to him, and he installed the glass himself and forgot he did it.

The loneliness of the senior leader is one of the most documented and least discussed facts of ministry. Pastors leave the work in great numbers, and when Barna asked those who had considered quitting what weighed on them, more than two in five named loneliness and isolation among the reasons (Barna 2021). We acknowledge this loneliness with a kind of sympathy that does nothing, the way we acknowledge that the work is hard. What we rarely do is look at where the loneliness comes from, because the source is uncomfortable. The loneliness of the senior seat is not only something done to the leader. It is largely something the leader does to himself, through power, and the cure he reaches for makes it worse.

Let me steel-man the leader who keeps his distance, because his reasons are not foolish and I have used every one of them. He will tell you, correctly, that he cannot be fully transparent with people he supervises, that there are confidences he must keep, that a leader who falls apart in front of his team destabilizes the whole team. He will tell you that authority requires a measure of separateness, that the captain cannot drink with the crew, that someone has to carry what cannot be shared. And he is right about all of it. The seat does require a real and necessary solitude. Some of the distance is the cost of the office, and pretending otherwise is its own kind of dishonesty.

But he has done something with that legitimate truth that turns it into a prison. He has taken the necessary solitude of the role and quietly expanded it into a total isolation that serves his power rather than his people. There is a difference between the loneliness that comes from carrying confidences and the loneliness that comes from never letting anyone see you need anything. The first is the cost of leadership. The second is the fruit of pride dressed as duty. He has confused them on purpose, because the second kind protects an image, and the image has become more precious to him than the relationships, and he calls the whole thing the loneliness of command when half of it is the loneliness of self-protection.

The text I want to carry is the long, sad arc of Saul, the first king of Israel, because no story in Scripture shows more plainly what power does to a man who uses it to protect himself. Saul began among the people, hiding among the baggage on the day he was chosen, a head taller than everyone and somehow still shy of the seat (1 Samuel 10:22-23 ESV). But once the crown was on him the seat began to close around him. When the women sang that David had struck down his ten thousands and Saul his thousands, the king eyed David from that day on (1 Samuel 18:9 ESV), and the eyeing never stopped. He grew suspicious of his own son, of his own servants, of the one man at court who loved him most, until he sat in his hall with a spear in his hand and no friend left in the room. Read what isolated him. Not the office. The office did not have to do this to him. What isolated Saul was a power he used to guard his standing instead of to serve his people, and the more he guarded it the more alone he became, until the lonely seat had swallowed him whole. That is the medicine taken in reverse, the warning written across a king's whole reign.

Because here is what power does to most of us, and the social science is as old as the church's amnesia about it. Edwin Friedman observed that leaders become isolated not primarily because others push them away but because they stop being honestly engaged, hiding behind the role, managing impressions, surrounding themselves with people who will not contradict them (Friedman 2007). The lonely leader has often, without admitting it, selected for agreement. He has promoted the people who affirm him and grown cool toward the ones who push, and over years he has built a court rather than a team, and a court is the loneliest place on earth because everyone in it is performing for the king. The isolation he laments is the harvest of choices he made one staffing decision at a time.

The history here runs deep and it indicts our whole model. The cult of the singular visionary pastor, the leader as charismatic founder whose voice cannot be questioned, took its modern shape in the church growth movement of the nineteen seventies and eighties and hardened into the celebrity pastor era that followed. We built churches around one magnetic personality and then watched, decade after decade, as those personalities fell, in moral collapse and in burnout and in the slow corrosion of men who had no peers because they had been elevated above everyone they knew. The architecture that made them powerful is the same architecture that made them alone. We keep building it. We keep being surprised when it produces the same wreckage it has always produced.

Henri Nouwen saw the spiritual mechanism under all of it, and he named the temptation with a precision that still stings. He wrote that the great seduction of Christian leadership is the temptation to power, to be the one in control, and that this temptation is so dangerous precisely because it is so easy to confuse the desire to rule with the desire to serve (Nouwen 1989). The antidote he prescribed was not better self-protection or more self-care. It was confession and community, the deliberate placing of oneself among people to whom one is accountable and before whom one is known, the refusal to lead alone. The lonely pastor has often medicated his loneliness with more control, and control is the drug that deepens the disease it pretends to treat.

Here is the reversal, and it is the hinge of everything. The solution to the loneliness of power is not more power and it is not less responsibility. It is vulnerability exercised from within the power, the choice to let someone see you while you still hold the authority. Where Saul guarded the throne until it isolated him, David, for all his sins, kept the throne and kept being known, wept openly, bound his soul to Jonathan, let the prophet Nathan walk in and tell him to his face that he was the man. This is terrifying, because we believe that to be seen as needy is to forfeit the right to lead. The cross says the reverse. The One with all authority in heaven and earth knelt and was stripped and let himself be seen at his most exposed, and he did not lose his authority by descending. He revealed it. Authority that cannot be seen needing is not authority, it is insecurity holding a title, and everyone on the staff can feel the difference even when they cannot name it.

What this asks of us is concrete and costly. It asks the senior leader to build, on purpose, a set of relationships outside his chain of command where he is not the pastor but simply a man who needs God, peers who can tell him the truth because their livelihood does not depend on his mood. It asks him to find a spiritual director or a soul friend, what Ruth Haley Barton calls the company of others who will help him discern his own deceptions, because the leader cannot see his own blind spots by definition and will go down with them if no one is permitted close enough to point (Barton 2008). And it asks him to stop curating a staff of admirers and start keeping the people who push back, treating their resistance as a gift instead of a threat.

I have lived on both sides of the glass, and the difference is not subtle once you have felt it. There were years when I told myself the distance between me and my staff was the dignity of the office, and what it actually was, underneath, was fear of being found out, the dread that if anyone got close enough they would discover I was less than the man who stood on the platform. So I kept everyone at the range of admiration, which is a safe and lonely range, and I mistook the safety for wisdom. What broke it was not a strategy. It was a few men outside my church who refused to be impressed by me, who asked how my marriage was and would not accept the sermon-version of the answer, and who slowly taught me that being known by a few is the only thing that makes being admired by many survivable. Bonhoeffer wrote that the person who cannot bear to be alone should beware of community, and that the person who cannot bear community should beware of being alone, because we need both and we will be destroyed by whichever one we use to flee the other (Bonhoeffer 1954). The lonely leader has used the crowd to flee the few, and it is killing him by the inch.

The lonely seat will not be cured by sympathy and it will not be cured by stepping down. It will be cured, if it is cured at all, by the slow and humbling work of letting yourself be known by people you cannot control, which is the only kind of being known that counts. Most of us would rather stay lonely than do that, because the loneliness, for all its pain, lets us keep the image intact. We choose the glass. We sit behind it and ache and call it the price of leadership, when half the time it is the price of pride.

Saul died on a mountain with no one left who could reach him, a king who had spent his whole reign making sure of it. Put down the power you are hiding behind, and you might not end there.

### Works Cited

Barna Group. 2021. 38% of U.S. Pastors Have Thought About Quitting Full-Time Ministry in the Past Year. Ventura, CA: Barna Group.

Barton, Ruth Haley. 2008. Strengthening the Soul of Your Leadership: Seeking God in the Crucible of Ministry. Downers Grove: InterVarsity Press.

Bonhoeffer, Dietrich. 1954. Life Together. Translated by John W. Doberstein. New York: Harper and Row.

Friedman, Edwin H. 2007. A Failure of Nerve: Leadership in the Age of the Quick Fix. New York: Seabury Books.

Nouwen, Henri J. M. 1989. In the Name of Jesus: Reflections on Christian Leadership. New York: Crossroad.

chapters.title: When to Fire Someone in Ministry
chapters.summary: The cruelest thing a pastor can do to a staff member is keep him on a year past the point where everyone but him already knows.
chapters.body:
The conversation everyone is dreading has already happened a hundred times. It has happened in the car on the way home, when the executive pastor's wife asked how it went and he said nothing and stared at the road. It has happened in the elder meeting, in the long pause after someone says his name. It has happened in the worship leader's own gut at two in the morning. The only place it has not happened is the one place it needs to happen, which is across a desk, in daylight, with the words said plainly. We will keep almost anyone for almost any length of time to avoid that one room.

Firing someone in ministry is harder than firing someone anywhere else, and we should say why instead of pretending otherwise. In a normal job, the relationship is contractual. In a church, the relationship is covenantal, or it feels that way. You prayed together. You buried his father. His kids call you by a nickname. You stood in front of the congregation and said God had called this person to this work, and now you are sitting across from him preparing to say it is over. The language of calling and the language of employment are tangled together, and we use the tangle as an excuse to do nothing.

Let me give the case for patience its full strength, because it is a strong case and I have hidden behind it. Grace is the center of what we preach. We believe people can change. We believe the Spirit is not finished with anyone. We have all known a leader who was struggling in month eight and thriving in month twenty, and we are right to fear the kind of pastor who fires fast and prays slow. Scripture is full of restoration, of Peter rebuilt on a beach after he had failed at the worst possible moment. A church that cuts its people loose at the first sign of weakness is not a church, it is a firm with a steeple. The patient pastor is protecting something real.

But grace and clarity are not enemies, and we treat them as if they were. The patient pastor has performed a sleight of hand on himself. He has decided that keeping the failing staff member is the gracious choice, when in fact it is often the cowardly one wearing grace as a costume. Grace toward the underperforming worship leader is not the only grace in the room. There is also the grace owed to the volunteers he is exhausting, the grace owed to the congregation he is no longer serving, the grace owed to the man himself, who deserves to know the truth while he is still young enough to find the thing he is actually built for. By calling my avoidance grace, I was spending other people's grace to protect my own comfort.

The text I want to carry is the appointing of the seven in Acts, because it shows that ministry roles exist for a function and not as a reward. The widows were being neglected in the daily distribution, and the apostles did not say the men currently failing at the task deserved patience. They said the work had to be done, and they sought out men full of the Spirit and of wisdom to do it (Acts 6:3 ESV). The role served the people. When the role stops serving the people, the role has to change hands, and the kindness is owed first to the people the role exists for. We have inverted this. We treat the staff position as belonging to the staff member, a possession we would be cruel to take away, when it was never his. It was the congregation's, on loan.

So when. Not for one bad season, and not for a personality you find tiring, and never for telling you the truth you did not want to hear. Fire for a sustained gap between the work and the person that prayer and coaching and time have not closed, when you have named it clearly more than once and given a real path and watched the path go unwalked. Fire for character, faster than you want to, because a gifted manipulator does more damage in a church than an honest underperformer ever will. Fire when keeping someone requires you to lie, to the elders about how it is going, to the congregation about why numbers are slipping, to the person himself about a future that is not coming. The lie is the signal. When you are lying to keep the peace, the peace is already gone.

The history of how we got so timid is worth tracing. The professionalization of ministry, which gathered speed across the twentieth century and accelerated after the church growth movement of the nineteen seventies built the multi-staff church, gave us employees without giving us the stomach to manage them. We borrowed the human resources department's vocabulary, the performance plan and the documented warning, but we kept a theology of the pastorate that treats every staff member as an ordained brother whose removal is a kind of excommunication. So we freeze. We have the corporate tools and the covenantal nerves, and the two cancel out, and the failing leader stays for three years while everyone suffers and calls it love.

Edwin Friedman saw this paralysis everywhere he looked, and he named its real cause. He said the chronically anxious system will always pressure the leader to relieve its anxiety, and the most anxious members will set the agenda, so the leader who cannot tolerate someone else's pain will be ruled by whoever is most willing to inflict it on him (Friedman 2007). The pastor who cannot fire is not more loving. He is less differentiated. He has let the discomfort of one hard conversation hold an entire church hostage. The failure of nerve does not look like failure. It looks like patience. That is what makes it so durable.

Here is the reversal that took me too long to learn. The kindest thing is almost always the earlier thing. The longer you wait, the worse the eventual conversation gets for everyone, especially the person you are protecting. Keep a man two years past the point of fit and you have not given him grace, you have given him two years of failing publicly, two years of his confidence eroding, two years of a marriage straining under a job he cannot do, before you finally say what you could have said with dignity at month nine. Delay does not soften the blow. It compounds it and then delivers it anyway, with interest he had no idea he was accruing.

Before the day comes, the cross has to do its work on you, and it does it as law before it does it as grace. The law first. The reason you cannot have this conversation is that you need this man to walk out still thinking well of you, and that need is an idol, the same idol the apostles refused when they would not let the neglected widows go on being neglected to spare anyone's feelings. You have made your own reputation as a kind employer into a small god, and it is costing the very people the role exists to serve. That is sin, and naming it as sin is the only thing that breaks its grip. The grace second. The cross says your standing was settled by Another before you ever managed a single staff member, bought in blood you did not spill, so you do not have to purchase this man's approval with one more year of his slow failure. You are free to tell the truth precisely because the verdict over you is not his to give. The leader who has heard that law and received that grace can deliver hard news from a settled place and not from anger, because he is no longer secretly trying to make the other person agree that he is fair. Tell the truth plainly. Own your part in waiting too long. Be generous with severance and time and a real reference, because how you end a tenure preaches to everyone still on staff about what you actually believe. Ruth Haley Barton writes that leaders have to attend to their own souls precisely so that their decisions flow from God and not from their own unexamined fear (Barton 2008). The firing done from a settled soul is a different act than the firing done from panic, even when the words are the same.

There is one more place we hide, and it is the holiest-sounding excuse of all. We say we are waiting on the Lord. We say we have not yet received clarity, that we are praying for wisdom, that we do not want to run ahead of God. And sometimes that is true and good. But often the language of discernment is the language of paralysis with a stained-glass window in front of it. Ruth Haley Barton writes that we have to be honest about the difference between genuine waiting on God and the spiritualized procrastination that lets us avoid a decision we already know we have to make (Barton 2008). The Spirit who gave us wisdom also gave us the courage to act on it. When the clarity has been sitting in your chest for six months and you are still calling it discernment, the thing you are waiting on is not God. It is your own willingness to be disliked.

The goal was never to be a man who can fire easily. The goal is to be a man who can tell the truth in love when love and truth both cost something. Most of us are not too quick to let people go. We are too slow, and we baptize the slowness, and the people we claim to be protecting pay for our comfort.

Grace tells the truth in time. Cowardice waits for it to die.

### Works Cited

Barton, Ruth Haley. 2008. Strengthening the Soul of Your Leadership: Seeking God in the Crucible of Ministry. Downers Grove: InterVarsity Press.

Friedman, Edwin H. 2007. A Failure of Nerve: Leadership in the Age of the Quick Fix. New York: Seabury Books.

chapters.title: Why Churches Close, and What Comes Next
chapters.summary: A church does not die when it locks the door but years earlier, the day it stopped believing it had anything the lost could not get elsewhere.
chapters.body:
I have stood in a sanctuary the week before it closed. The pews were still there, the hymnals still in the racks, the offering plates stacked on a table in the narthex like dishes after the last guest has gone. An older woman walked me through it, naming the rooms, the nursery where her children had been dedicated, the kitchen where they had served funeral luncheons for sixty years. She was not crying. She had cried years earlier, she told me, when she first understood it was over, long before anyone said it aloud. That is the thing about a church closing. By the time the door is locked, the death is old news. The body was cooling for a decade while everyone kept setting the table.

We ask the wrong question when a church closes. We ask what went wrong at the end, as if the cause were proximate, a bad pastor, a building too big, a neighborhood that changed. Those are symptoms, and treating symptoms as causes is how we keep getting blindsided. The real question is harder and older. Why does a community that began with people willing to die for a crucified man end as a few faithful souls maintaining a building out of loyalty to the dead. The answer is rarely a scandal. The answer is usually a slow, respectable forgetting, a forgetting so gradual that no one in it could name the day it became fatal.

The data is not in dispute, and I will only use what is solid. Lifeway Research, working with denominational figures, estimated that roughly forty-five hundred Protestant churches closed in the United States in 2019 while about three thousand opened, a net loss in a single year (Earls 2021). Pew Research has tracked the share of Americans who claim no religion climbing from sixteen percent in 2007 to roughly twenty-eight percent by the early 2020s, the so-called nones now rivaling any single Christian tradition in size (Pew Research Center 2024). These are real numbers and they describe a real bleeding. But numbers explain that churches are closing. They do not explain why. For that you have to go further back than any chart reaches.

The strongest argument against pastoral hand-wringing deserves a fair hearing, because it is mostly right. The secularization theorists said this was coming and named the mechanism. Peter Berger argued for years that modernity dissolves the plausibility of belief, that when a society offers a thousand competing accounts of reality, no single sacred canopy can hold, and faith that once felt like the air becomes a choice that feels increasingly strange (Berger 1967, 127). On this account, churches close not because pastors failed but because the social conditions that made belief easy simply evaporated, and no amount of faithfulness could have held back a tide that size. There is real truth here, and pastors who pretend otherwise are lying to themselves. We did not cause the secular age and we cannot reverse it by trying harder. But Berger himself, to his great credit, recanted the strongest form of his own theory near the end of his life, conceding that the world had not become less religious, only that the West had, and that the simple story of inevitable decline did not survive contact with the actual planet (Berger 1999, 2). So the steel-manned version is not that secularization is a law of history. It is that secularization removed the social scaffolding that propped up nominal faith. And that distinction is the whole of the matter, because what secularization actually did was expose churches that had been living on scaffolding instead of on Christ.

Here is the text I cannot put down when I think about closed churches. To the church in Sardis, the risen Christ dictates a sentence that should make every pastor cold. I know your works. You have the reputation of being alive, but you are dead (Revelation 3:1 ESV). Sardis was a real congregation in a wealthy city, a church with a name, a brand, a standing. From the street it looked alive. The reputation was intact. And the verdict from the only One whose verdict counts was that the reputation had outlived the reality. That is how churches close. Not in a moment of dramatic apostasy but in a long stretch where the name stays alive after the life has left, where the reputation does the breathing the Spirit used to do. The closed church I walked through still had its name on the sign the week it died. Sardis always does.

Trace the root and the years line up. The slow death of the Western church did not begin with the nineties or the sixties. Mark Noll located a deeper failure in the way American Christianity, especially evangelicalism, had spent a century neglecting the life of the mind, building a faith long on feeling and short on the intellectual seriousness that could survive a hostile age (Noll 1994, 3). A church that cannot think cannot answer its children's questions, and a church that cannot answer its children loses them one confirmation class at a time, and the loss does not show on the attendance sheet for twenty years because the grandparents keep coming. By the time the demographics turn, the cause is three generations upstream. We buried our seriousness in 1925 and locked the door in 2019 and called it a building problem.

Now the reversal, because the gospel does not end at the autopsy. The most important fact about a closed church is the one we never say at the funeral. The closing of a congregation is not the closing of the kingdom. We grieve the building because we confused the building with the body, and we confused the body with the kingdom, and Christ never made either mistake. He told a parable about a seed that has to fall into the ground and die before it can bear any fruit at all (John 12:24 ESV). The seed that refuses to die stays a single seed, intact, respectable, alone, exactly like a church guarding its survival until survival is all it has left to worship. The churches that close having spent themselves on the lost are not the tragedy. The tragedy is the churches that close having spent themselves on staying open.

This is where the law has to land before any comfort comes. The law says that some churches close because of sin we would rather call circumstance. We loved our preferences more than our neighbors. We made the music, the carpet, the order of service into hills we defended while the mission field outside the doors went unvisited. I have sat in those meetings. I have watched a congregation spend its last energy fighting over a thing that would not matter in heaven, and I have stayed quiet when I should have named it, which makes me part of it. The law does not let me stand outside this. Andrew Root has written that the secular age has not only thinned belief but accelerated everything, leaving churches frantically busy and spiritually exhausted, mistaking activity for life (Root 2019, 6). The law says our busyness was not faithfulness. It was the death rattle of a body that no longer trusted the Spirit to do the breathing.

And then grace, which is the only word that makes a closed church bearable. The God we serve has never needed the institution to survive in order to keep His promise. He buried His own Son and the burial was not the end of the story but the hinge of it. So what comes next, after a church closes, is what has always come next when something falls into the ground in faith. The seed that died in one congregation rises in the people it formed, the children it baptized who carry the word into rooms that building never reached, the resources released to plant where the soil is ready. I have seen a closed church give its building to a young congregation that filled it within two years. The name on the sign changed. The kingdom did not lose a square foot.

Not every church should be saved. Some should be buried with honor, hands open, the way you bury a saint who finished the race. The sin is not in dying. The sin is in pretending to live while refusing to either repent or rest. Sardis could have woken up. The text begged her to. Wake up, and strengthen what remains and is about to die (Revelation 3:2 ESV). Some did. Some did not. The door locks either way. The kingdom does not.

The building was never the church. We knew that. We forgot it slowly, the way men forget the thing they cannot afford to remember.

### Works Cited

Berger, Peter L. 1967. The Sacred Canopy: Elements of a Sociological Theory of Religion. Garden City: Doubleday.

Berger, Peter L. 1999. The Desecularization of the World: Resurgent Religion and World Politics. Grand Rapids: Eerdmans.

Earls, Aaron. 2021. Protestant Church Closures Outpace Openings in U.S. Nashville: Lifeway Research.

Noll, Mark A. 1994. The Scandal of the Evangelical Mind. Grand Rapids: Eerdmans.

Pew Research Center. 2024. Religious Landscape Study. Washington: Pew Research Center.

Root, Andrew. 2019. The Pastor in a Secular Age: Ministry to People Who No Longer Need a God. Grand Rapids: Baker Academic.

chapters.title: Why Gen Z Is Coming Back to Church
chapters.summary: The young are not returning to be comforted but to be told the truth, and the church that flatters them will lose them again.
chapters.body:
A nineteen-year-old asked to meet me at a coffee shop last spring. He had been raised on nothing, no church, no catechism, a household where religion was treated the way you treat an old superstition, with a shrug. And he had spent two years reading, watching, arguing online, and now he sat across from me and said he thought it might all be true, the cross, the resurrection, the whole improbable claim, and he wanted to know if I believed it or just performed it. He was not looking for a welcome. He had welcomes everywhere. He was looking for someone who would not lie to him. I recognized him immediately, because I was him. I came to faith from atheism, and no one ever won me with comfort.

So I want to be careful with the headline, because the truth underneath it is more interesting than the headline.
